utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are rested, are you feeling fine? Counsel, you have the floor. I believe you wanted to go ahead with the video after which the Judges will have some questions. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. That is correct. We would like to proceed this morning with a video which is a compilation of many of the pieces of video and film that the Office of the Prosecutor has collected as evidence. While it could not possibly accurately portray what it was like to live in Sarajevo during the siege, it is intended as a type of slice of life of what it was like to live through the sniping and shelling. So with the court's permission we would like to have the lights dimmed and that particular video played. (The video was played)

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, do you have any final comments for the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, and all the Judges, I did not want with my testimony to provoke anybody's emotions. The facts about the siege and the strangulation of Sarajevo are well known more or less to everybody. I would like to point out, however, that we never lost hope in peace and justice. This Tribunal was founded to defend the principles of civilisations from the attack by war criminals. The onus is on you, Prosecutors and Judges, to take care of this huge historical responsibility. Whether barbarian principles will overcome, all international organisations are capable of bringing war criminals to justice and punish them appropriately. The justification for not doing something can always be found. We must do something. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes the Prosecution's presentation, your Honours. We would now open it up for questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bowers. Let me turn to fellow Judges: Judge Odio Benito, you have some questions? Please go right ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did your political party try to avoid the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What about the other political parties, did they try to avoid the war also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All parties worked on keeping the peace, except the Serbian Democratic Party led by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Many times you have used the expression "Karadzic's Serbs", that means that there are other kinds of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By saying "Karadzic's Serbs", I mean those who spent, who pursued the policy that brought about the situation in which crimes were committed. During the entire war there were about 40,000 Serbs living in Sarajevo which suffered in exactly the same way as other citizens of Sarajevo, together with them, and in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, in many towns, the victims of the war were Serbs, different from Karadzic's Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned 12,000 victims of this siege, among them 1600 children. Do you know how many women and how many men died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but roughly it is half and half.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Finally, sir, I beg your pardon for asking this, but after this horrible war, how do you see the future of your city, the future of your family and the future of your country as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see the future of my town, my country and my family as having begun already. In Sarajevo, it is much easier to live now than it was immediately after the agreement, the Dayton Agreement, was signed, but the hurdle to serious reconstruction of the country, to reconciliation, to reconstruction, are the war criminals that this court is to try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mayor Kupusovic, in one of the interviews you showed us we could hear Mr. Karadzic saying, "We could take Sarajevo any time". I remember that looking at Sarajevo from the hill. In your assessment, why did they not take Sarajevo and why did they inflict the siege on it for such a long time? What was the purpose of this whole operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am convinced that they could have entered Sarajevo and taken it the first few weeks of the war, the first few weeks of May when the siege started, but their goal was not to destroy the city completely, because at the same time there were offices and high officers of the United Nations and International Red Cross, many journalists. Their goal was to divide the city, to make one part of the city exclusively Muslim, another part exclusively Serbian and possibly another one Croatian. As they did not succeed in doing so at the beginning, then by a long siege they wanted to make life in the city impossible, so that the inhabitants of the city could feel hopelessness, to abandon their city so that the city as such would die. Afterwards, when they wanted to take the city, they could not do so without enormous human, technical and other losses on their own side.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. In your summary at the beginning, you mentioned that the Serbs were a minority compared to the Muslims. Did this minority suffer from any discrimination in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By no means. There were about 42 per cent of Muslims in Sarajevo and 33 per cent Serbs and about eight to nine per cent Catholics, Croatians, and other people from mixed marriages and others. But never in Sarajevo has there been any uneasiness for anyone else by somebody else, whether it was a Serb, a Romany, a Jew. In the villages around Sarajevo before the war the Serbs launched propaganda in order to cause the uneasiness of Serbs, to make it look as if they were jeopardised by the others. They never succeeded in doing so in the city, but, unfortunately, in mono-ethnic villages inhabited by Serbs exclusively, they succeeded in doing so. But this is a matter for the future when the civilian population returns to their normal views of life together.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: There were no clashes in the previous years between Serbs and Muslims in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there have never been any clashes, neither during the First World War or the Second World War in the town itself. There have never been inter-ethnic conflicts among the citizens of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Then what promoted the hostility? What influence was there to promote this hostility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is all tied with the plans for Greater Serbia which included annexing a large part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia. Wherever there was an absolute or relative majority of Serbs, according to those plans, all the Serbs were to live in one state and only Serbs in that particular state. Only the Serbs is the part that brought about the eviction and expelling of all the other people and the crimes that had to accompany such a goal. In that context, Sarajevo had to be divided for an enclave was to be left for non-Serbs which in due time would disappear, as was the case in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: We noticed in many interviews by Dr. Karadzic concerning Sarajevo; was also General Mladic involved in this siege of Sarajevo in certain ways?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He commanded all the troops of the Serbian army, of the Republika Srpska army, and he issued orders. Nothing could be done on the military plane without General Mladic and their media, the media of Republika Srpska, broadcast this news and this is a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mayor Kupusovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mayor, just a further one or two questions: during these four very long years there were a lot of negotiations about cease-fires. Did you participate personally in any of these negotiations and what was your impression? Did you think that there was serious negotiating taking place? What were your feelings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the first two years of siege, I participated in commissions for solving the problems related to water supply, supply of the electricity and natural gas. On the technical level, on the level of professionals, the arrangements were quite clear and proclamations for the water, the electricity and the gas and other essential infrastructure would not be used for war purposes. However, these arrangements usually fell flat after a certain time and later new arrangements were made. Later, as Mayor, I did not take part directly in these negotiations, but through my assistance on the technical level of Commissions for infrastructure, which were conducted by the representatives of the United Nations in Sarajevo. I think that these negotiations, that the representatives of the Serbian side did not have any intention to abide by them, because their goal was to show, to indicate, that they are the masters, the lords, of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a question about the city status. In the Dayton Agreement how does that status work? What is your view of that? How do you think it will work out in the future in the framework of the Dayton Accord, and also what your fellow countrymen think of that Agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sarajevo is one of several towns of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which multi-ethnic, a multi-ethnic structure has been preserved and an urban way of life, what had been defended throughout the siege of Sarajevo. According to the Dayton Accord, Sarajevo has been defined as the capital of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of Croats and Bosniaks, and the capital of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that very soon, although it has not happened yet, we will reach a definition of the canton of Sarajevo and the city of Sarajevo, and the district where all the institutions of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of both entities, will be based. It is essential that the basic public services return to normal operation, that the citizens start working and making a living, and then all these problems behind us will be behind us indeed, and we will have a future to look forward to.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kupusovic. I do not have any further questions. Fellow Judges, no further questions? Counsel, no questions? The Tribunal would like to thank you. Thank you very much indeed for your coming here. We are quite aware of the difficulties this has given rise to for you to go over all of this. We would like to thank you most heartily and wish you a safe trip home. We do hope that you will be able to reintegrate more or less normal life. Thank you again. I think we can usher the witness out, unless counsel for the Prosecution have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, would you like to take the floor first? No? The Trial Chamber learnt on the first day of the opening of this public hearing the actual charges against the accused Karadzic and Mladic. The decision was read on first day and it consists of inviting as amicus curiae two personalities for the present hearing. The moment has come for the Trial Chamber to hear the presentation of Madam Christine Cleiren. We have asked her to attend this meeting -- could you please wait one moment, one moment; I would like to finish before -- the Chamber has asked Christine Cleiren who is a member of the Expert Commission which was set up by the Security Council to appear as amicus curiae to participate in this discussion, to explain to us her findings in that Commission and also to tell us about the practices of rape and how it is used as part of an overall policy for ethnic cleansing. I now invite Mrs. Cleiren to be taken to the witness stand. For technical facilities, we will ask her to go there, but, please, I would like to remind you that she is not a witness but an amicus curiae so she will not have to swear an oath. So, please, if you could take your head sets and be seated? MRS. CHRISTINE CLEIREN TOOK THE WITNESS STAND

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Cleiren, I will not repeat what I have just said, but this is how we envisage the next statement. Do you hear me? Do you hear me? Let me remind you that in the Rules of this court, there is Article 74 which states that a Trial Chamber can, if it thinks it is necessary in the interest of good administration of justice, invite any organisation, anybody, any individual, to give a statement on any questions which they deem relevant. So I know that you have received the letter of invitation in order to come to the Chamber. First of all, we would like to thank you for coming here today. I think the way we wish to structure the forthcoming hour or so will be done in the following way. You will introduce yourself, you will tell us who you are, what you have done, why you were appointed to be part of the Commission. Then you will make the statement which you think is useful for us and you will tell us your findings which you have got when a member of the Commission of Experts. After that, we will concentrate on the points which initiated this invitation, that is to say, on the practice of rape or sexual violence or assault since 1992. I would like to know the conclusions you had in that Commission, your personal conclusions and findings. Then the Trial Chamber, the one who asked you to come, will ask you questions if they think it is necessary. This has been done also in the cases by the witnesses called by the Office of the Prosecutor. Then I will ask the Prosecutor to ask him whether he has any further questions he wishes to put to you. Mrs. Cleiren, please speak freely. Do not worry. Tell us everything you know openly, feel free. You are in front of an International Tribunal, a court body, so please feel, tell us frankly and openly and we will listen to what you have to say. MRS. CHRISTINE CLEIREN: Thank you, your Honour, I will start to introduce myself. I usually be a professor in criminal law and criminal procedure in the Netherlands at the -- University. I was a member of the Commission of Experts during eight months from October 1993 until the ending of the Commission. I was appointed in that Commission after the Chairman of the Commission, Kalshoven, resigned and after another member of the Commission, Professor Opsahl, died. Then in October 1993, two new members were appointed, Judge Greve and myself. In this Commission some tasks were shared, and that often with regard to that tasks it is useful to say here that I was not explicitly responsible for the sexual assault investigation or sexual assault studies. On the contrary, most of that responsibility for the sexual assault investigation was with the Chairman, Professor Bassionni, and the only responsibility I had for this special team, this special subject, was the legal study that is part of the annexes of the final report of the Commission. I will try to give you an overview of the activities of the Commission of Experts with regard to sexual assault and rape and its conclusions on that subject. The Commission took several approaches to the questions that raise on this subject. It prepared a legal study to consider the criteria for applying international humanitarian law instruments in this context. This study dealt on the one hand with the possibilities and on the other hand with the limitations of the law as it applies to these specific crimes. Besides, the Commission collected material. It received information from a wide range of sources, governments, international organisations, non-governmental organisations, religious groups, women's groups, private individuals and the media. In addition, the Commission carried out a field investigation to interview victims and witnesses, specifically to answer the question if there was a pattern of sexual abuse, of systematic sexual violence. I will present you the patterns of rape and sexual assault which, according to the Commission's Final Report, can be identified by these findings, and the common threads run through the cases reported and the systematic character of at least part of these cases, but not before expressing some reservation and some caution with regard to these findings. In the first place, the Commission did not have a complete view on the full extent of sexual violence for, among others, the following reasons. The Commission did its work while the conflict was ongoing. Second, we all know that reporting sexual violence is difficult and this problem is exaggerated in war where there is a breakdown in law and order and perpetrators are often soldiers. The victims may have little confidence in finding justice and many seem to be reluctant to report their experience. Victims and witnesses fear the attackers. They are ashamed and humiliated by what happened and many of them do not dare to talk fearing the traumatic experience of passing through again. Another reason for being cautious is that the information the Commission received contained allegations. However, the reliability and the credibility of reports and testimonies could not be verified by the Commission caused by various reasons. Consequently, one must be extremely careful to draw conclusions based on individual cases, among others, for the following reasons. Individuals, as well as groups, may be driven by political or personal revenge or by encouraging groups to report sexual violence. Second, as time goes by, it becomes increasingly difficult to sort out the true stories from the false ones. It is well known phenomenon and also occurred in the Yugoslavian case that some people identified themselves that extreme with victims of sexual violence that they state de auditu-stories as their own experience. There are indications that sexual violence was reported by the parties in the conflict as an element of propaganda. The information in the reports was second or third hand, and much of this of it was very general. In spite of these remarks, the Commission had reason to state that sexual assault and rape were committed across widely, partly as the result of individual or small group conduct without command direction and without an overall policy, but partly as the result of an overall policy. This conclusion is suggested by a number of recurrent patterns, the cumulative effect of similar and analogous statements and the common threads in the cases reported. In particular, the cumulation of reports and statements supported and confirmed the view of the Commission. According to the Commission's Final Report, five patterns of rape and sexual assault can be identified by the findings of the Commission. To inform you as adequately as possible, I will partly cite some paragraphs of the text of the final report of the Commission on this subject. I will take them paragraphs 245 to 249. The five patterns we distinguish are sexual violence with looting and intimidation. That is the first pattern. The second pattern you can say is sexual violence during fighting. The third is sexual violence in detention facilities, and the fourth sexual violence in special rape camps, and a fifth sexual violence in brothel houses. I will start with the first. Then I will cite part of the report. Paragraph 254: "The first pattern involves individuals or small groups committing sexual assault in conjunction with looting and intimidation of the target ethnic group. This is before any widespread or generalised fighting breaks out in the region. Tensions in an area grow and members of the ethnic group controlling the regional government begin to terrorise their neighbours. "Two or men break into a house, intimidate the residents, steal their property, beat them and often rape the females. Some of the reported rapes are singular and some multiple. In either case, there is often a gang atmosphere where the abuses are part of the same event and all attackers participate even if they do not sexually assault the victims". That is the first pattern in which some cases or a large group of cases can be placed. "The second pattern of rape involves individuals or small groups committing sexual assault in conjunction with fighting in an area, often including the rape of women in public. When forces attack a town or a village, the population is rounded up and divided by sex and age. Some women are raped in their homes as the attacking forces secure the area. Others are selected after the round up and raped publicly. The population of the village is then transported to camps. "The third pattern of rape involves individuals or groups sexual assaulting people in detention because they have access to the people. Once the population of a town or village has been rounded up, men are either executed or sent off to camps, while women are generally sent off to separate camps. Soldiers, camp guards, paramilitaries and even civilians may be allowed to enter the camp, pick out women, take them away, rape them and then either kill them or return them to the site. "Reports frequently refer to gang rape, while beatings and torture accompany most of the reported rapes. Survivors report that some women are taken out alone, and some are taken out in groups. Though this is the general pattern, there are also many allegations that women are raped in front of other internees, or that other internees are forced to sexually abuse each other. In camps where men are detained, they are also subjected to sexual abuse. During the Commission's interviewing process, 15 people were interviewed whose major allegations related to the same detention camp. Some witnesses were men, and all of the women victims had been raped. The women were sometimes gang raped by, or in the presence of, the Camp Commander. Guards from the external ring of security around the camp and soldiers who were strangers to the camp would be allowed access to the camp for rape". Then the fourth pattern, the sexual violence in special rape camps. "The fourth pattern of rape involves individuals or groups committing sexual assaults against women for the purposes of terrorising and humiliating them often as part of the policy of "ethnic cleansing". Survivors of some camps report that they believe they were detained for the purpose of rape. In those camps, all of the women are raped quite frequently, often in front of other internees, and usually accompanied by beatings and torture. Some captors also state that they trying to impregnate the women. Pregnant women are detained until it is too late for them to obtain an abortion". Then the fifth pattern, that is, the sexual violence in what they call brothel houses. "The fifth pattern of rape involves detention of women in hotels or similar facilities for the sole purpose of sexually entertaining soldiers, rather than causing a reaction in the women. These women are reportedly more often killed than exchanged, unlike women in other camps. One woman interviewed was detained in a private house with a number of other women for six months. The women were of mixed ethnicity. All the women were raped when soldiers returned from the frontline every 15 days. "The witness was told that the women had to do this because the women in other camps (which the witness named and which has been documented by other information gathered) were exhausted". So these were the five patterns the Commission identified out of the material they received. Summarising, we can say that sexual violence seemed to be committed widespread. Part of the report of the rape and sexual assault cases are clearly the result of an individual or a small group conduct, without evidence of common direction or an overall policy. However, many cases seem to be part of an overall pattern. This conclusion is, among others, based on the following: the information the Commission had on sexual violence in Bosnia-Herzegovina indicates that this practice was widespread. Over 80 cities and villages are alleged to have been the site of rape. In approximately 30 cities or villages, rape I appears to have been concentrated. It was hardly possible to determine if these areas were the only areas of concentrated rape. Some factors indicate a link between military action and rape and, in particular, military action design to displace populations. Furthermore, these seemingly organised rape were conducted in multiple, disparate locations and within a fairly close period of time, between spring and late fall 1992. Moreover, there seems to be a contemporaneous existence of systematic rape and other violations of international humanitarian law in the same regions. Violative conduct occurred simultaneously in prison camps, in the field and in the occupied areas. For example, while prison camps were the scene of large scale killing and torture, they were also the scene of reported systematic rape. So, you can try to say that there were centres of action of violence, of violative conduct. The Final Report of the Commission continues then with the common threads that run through the cases reported whether they were outside or in detention context. I will cite for you paragraph 250 on the common threads: "(a) Rapes seem to occur in conjunction with efforts to displace the targeted ethnic group from the region. This may involve heightened shame and humiliation by raping victims in front of adult and minor family members, in front of other detainees or in public places, or by forcing family members to rape each other. Young women and virgins are targeted for rape, along with prominent members of the community and educated women. "(b) Many reports state that perpetrators said they were ordered to rape, or that the aim was to ensure that the victims and their families would never want to return to the area. Perpetrators tell female victims that they will bear children of the perpetrator's ethnicity, that they must become pregnant, and then hold them in custody until it is too late for the victims to get an abortion. Victims are threatened that if they ever tell anyone, or anyone what has happened, the perpetrators will hunt them down and kill them. "(c) Large groups of perpetrators subject victims to multiple rapes and sexual assault. In detention, perpetrators go through the detention centres with flashlights at night selecting and return them the next morning, while camp commander often know about, and sometimes participate in. "(d) Victims may be sexually abused with foreign objects like broken glass, bottles, guns and truncheons. Castrations are performed through crude means such as forcing other detainees to bite off a prisoner's testicles". This threat we can identify on the material. Summarising, or trying to summarise what we had as basic information for this conclusion, is that there were great similarities among practices in non-contiguous geographic areas; there was simultaneous commission of other humanitarian law violations; simultaneous military activity; simultaneous activity to displace civilian populations and common elements of the commission of rape and sexual assault, like maximising shame and humiliation not only to the victim but also to the victim's community. The presence of these factors strongly suggest that the systematic rape and sexual assault policy existed. For the general conclusions of the Commission on this subject, I will cite some elements of paragraphs 251 and 253: "Rape has been reported to have been committed by all sides to the conflict. However, the large number of reported victims have been Bosnian Muslims, and the largest number of alleged perpetrators have been Bosnian Serbs. There are few reports of rape and sexual assault between members of the same ethnic group". 252: "In Bosnia, some of the reported rape and sexual assault cases committed by Serbs, mostly against Muslims, are clearly the result of individual or small group conduct without evidence of command direction or an overall policy. However, many more seem to be a part of an overall pattern whose characteristics include similarities among practices in the areas", and all the other factors I already mentioned. Paragraph 253: "These patterns strongly suggest that a systematic rape policy existed in certain areas, but it remains to be proven whether such an overall policy which existed which was to apply to all non-Serbs. It is clear that some level of organisation and group activity was required to carry out many of the alleged rapes. Furthermore, rape and sexual assault should be examined in the context of the practice of "ethnic cleansing" which is discussed in paragraphs 129 to 150 and the practices in detention camps discussed in paragraph 230. When viewed in these contexts, it is clear that grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions occurred, as did other violations of international humanitarian law". So, an important element in the conclusions of the Commission is that part of the sexual violence only can be understood within the context of the practice in the various camps and related to the broader concept of "ethnic cleansing". I will cite a part of paragraph 133 of ethnic cleansing and 134: "The manner in which the policy of 'ethnic cleansing' is carried out by Serbs in Bosnia is consistent throughout a certain geographic area represented by an arc ranging from northern Bosnia and covering areas in eastern and western Bosnia adjoining the Serb Krajina area in Croatia. "The practice of "ethnic cleansing" is carried out in strategic areas linking Serbia proper with Serb inhabited areas in Bosnia and Croatia. This strategic factor is significantly relevant to understanding why the policy has been carried out in certain areas and not in others. "The coercive means used to remove the civilian population from the above-mentioned strategic areas include mass murder, torture, rape and other forms of sexual assault", so far. Through the international media, public attention was focused on the practice of sexual assault and rape in the former Yugoslavia at the end of 1992. Reports of systematic rape started to significantly decline in 1993. By the summer of 1993 very few cases were being reported. These facts and this factor can indicate for the Commission the ability of the leadership to restrain and prevent such conduct when public pressure mounted, and thus can be relevant to the issue of command responsibility. You can find it back in paragraph 237: "This could lead to the conclusion that there was an overriding policy advocating the use of rape as a method of "ethnic cleansing", rather than a policy of omission, tolerating the widespread commission of rape". Referring to the camps, it can be important to point out that the Commission had rather detailed information on Bosnian Serb Republic camps. These camps are ultimately intended to achieve ethnic cleansing. The major part of the sexual violence seems to be occurred in this kind of detention facilities. For the practice in detention camps, I can mention paragraphs 223 and 230 of the Report. In paragraph 132, the Commission emphasises with regard to the policy of ethnic cleansing that responsibility for criminal conduct must be determined on an individuals basis. This remark brings me to the question of command responsibility with regard to sexual violence. Sometimes camp commanders or field military commanders explicitly ordered their subordinates to commit acts of sexual violence. In these cases, the individual commander's criminal responsibility is without doubt. In other cases, they fail to prevent sexual assault and did not punish perpetrators when their crimes were disclosed. This is a violation of a commander's duties and makes the commander criminally responsible under international law. The responsibility can be followed all the way up the chain of command, to those who planned the policy, while pretending to know nothing about it. There is no doubt that there was a consistent failure to prevent the commission of such crimes and to prosecute and punish their perpetrators. I think I will leave it here. This was, in general, the position of the Commission and the material which was the basis for their conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Madam, in our concern not to stop the consistency of your statement which has now been concluded, the Trial Chamber has decided to have a break (which we have every morning roughly in the middle of hearing), so we will adjourn now and we will start again at 11.30. At that time we will ask you some questions. The hearing is now adjourned. (11.10 a.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time) (11.30 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As I told you just before the break, the Tribunal would like to ask you some questions. I first give the floor to Judge Odio Benito. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Professor Cleiren, have you written and published articles dealing with rape and other forms of sexual assault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wrote a part of the Annex of the Commission's Report, so that is Annex II of all the Annexes. It is a legal study about rape. I wrote an article in a journal, The Criminal Law Forum on the applicability of several Articles of the Geneva Conventions, the violations of law, the crimes against humanity, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Professor Cleiren, is it fair to assume that the outrage about the alleged massive rapes committed against women was one of the main forces leading to the creation of the Commission of Experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have not enough information of that background to give you a clear answer on this point.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In the Commission's report it is stated, paragraph 142, I quote: "There is sufficient evidence to conclude that the practices of 'ethnic cleansing' were not coincidental, sporadic or carried out by disorganised groups or bands of civilians who could not be controlled by the Bosnian Serb leadership". What evidence did the Commission use to arrive at this conclusion and how does rape fit into the practices of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I try to give a clear answer, but it is not easy, as I tried to illustrate in my presentation. Important is for the conclusion of ethnic cleansing, the aspect I told on, let us say, the strategy, the strategic factor, that the Serb -- that the practice of ethnic cleansing is carried out in strategic areas linking the Serbia proper with the Serbian inhabited areas. This strategic factor is relevant, is significantly relevant, to recognise the elements of policy, also the elements of policy in the sexual assault cases. Besides that, the brutality with which these acts of violence were carried out is important. They were carried out by -- as I say, this is evidenced by a large number of killings, torture, rape etc., and this complex of violative means indicates at least the target of an assumed policy. But, nevertheless, in my opinion, it is hardly to say which and how much evidence is required to state that there was a policy of ethnic cleansing. However, the foregoing elements, let us say, the strategy that they used and the brutality with which it was combined, and that combined with the number of reports and the accumulation of similar statements in it, and the accumulation of similar reports, that indicates that there must be a policy or part of a policy. The second question you ask is, how did rape fit into the practice of the ethnic cleansing? It can be said that rape has been used, not only as an attack on the individuals, but that it was intended to humiliate, to ashame, to degrade the entire ethnic group. There are reports of public rapes, for example, in front of a whole village, old women, children, young children. Also, there are reports that the rape, rape and sexual violence, was used to let people flee from their region. So, then you can say that it is part of a policy of ethnic cleansing. Another argument can be that the perpetrators often told their victims that they had to become pregnant or that they held them in custody, that it was too late for the victim to have an abortion. Also, often it is told that the women -- often the women were told that they would have children of the perpetrator's identity and the perpetrator's ethnicity, and they would be a living remember of what happened in this war. Some perpetrators had declared that they were ordered to rape. So, all these arguments together, you can think that rape was part of this policy of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In your expert opinion, how widespread was the practice of rape in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was rather widespread. As I told you, the information we had contained statements of about 80 villages and cities. Their rape was often reported, and it was spread over the whole, let us say, the whole region, but especially in the strategic region that I told you before, the arc between the Serbian and the Serbian inhabitants in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Professor Cleiren, were there also rapes not necessarily associated with ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I guess there are; the Commission also stated that there were cases of rape and sexual violence without being part of a policy of an ethnic cleansing. In several cases, it is not possible to make a link to, let us say, a party or soldiers or a paramilitary organisation. In other cases, it is fairly clear that there was a link. But especially certainly in cases, I try to give you some practical information, there were cases that the army came in a village, they take off the men and the women stayed there with children and old people. Part of these women is raped, not only by soldiers, but also by the people who lived there. It is hardly to say that there was a plan to do this, but it was the factual situation that brought it with it. So I guess you can say there were individual rape cases also. Maybe it is possible to say that they were, effectively, caused by the breakdown of law and order, so they caused their own cases of sexual violence.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Professor Cleiren, in addition to the possible practice of rape for the purposes of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia-Herzegovina, could you tell us briefly what is the history of women under armed conflict with respect to rape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. I am wondering if you could illustrate to the court as an expert witness, as you are, the briefly what is the history for women under armed conflict with respect to rape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a well-known fact that in all wars in history rape is used or, let us say, rapes occurred. It is not quite clear if rape is always used as a factor or an instrument in war. It is impossible to say that it is partly caused by the fact that there were hardly investigations of the rape cases in history. But, nevertheless, it is quite clear that it happened oft and hardly in every war.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In your expert opinion, Professor Cleiren, under what circumstances within a war context can rape be considered as a grave breach, according to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Under what circumstances within a war context can rape be considered as a grave breach, according to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, it is important, of course, that it is a conflict with an international character.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But besides that, I guess there are -- I guess it is possible to consider rape as a grave breach, and I think it is important to recognise rape as a grave breach of the Conventions of Geneva. The conditions under which -- it depends on the interpretation of all the conditions of the grave breaches. I guess it is too complex to illustrate all the arguments, to use it here. I tried to explain these arguments in my article in Criminal Law Forum. I will hand it over to you afterwards. But the real conditions for the cases is -- I try to answer, it is not easy to say -- I think it is important that especially the individual cases can be prosecuted and punished by the Grave Breaches, and especially those cases that are not so easy to bring under the widespread systematic rape as necessary for the Crimes Against Humanity. So the Grave Breaches are in this perspective, they are easier to prove, and I guess it can be useful to bring these facts under the Grave Breaches. It is also a principle point to bring up on the Grave Breaches because, let us say, it is a form of recognising the status and the qualification of rape in war. So also from that perspective it is important to recognise rape as a Grave Breach and the same is for Violations of War and Customs of War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Cleiren, for your statement. No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn to my other side, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Professor Cleiren, you mentioned five patterns of rape; merely one of these patterns cannot be the result of individual activity, and the rape for ethnic cleansing; the other forms perhaps you mentioned, intimidating, looting and so on, this might have occurred in previous conflicts and could be individual, but can you say that rape for ethnic cleansing is the result of a general policy from the higher command authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand well, you ask if the -----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Shall I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe, yes, OK.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: If the other forms of rape which you mentioned could exist also without a higher policy or a command policy, can you say that ethnic cleansing or rape for ethnic cleansing can also be the result of individual activity or has it to represent a general policy by the high command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is important in the rape cases that even if there is no command there can be a form of ethnic cleansing, especially in the cases of the camps, for instance, because in the camps men were allowed to come in in some camps and they could rape women and the commanders of the camp did not prevent it. They failed to prevent this kind of conduct and they did not punish the commanders for doing it. So, if you treat this chain of command up, then you will have, let us say, the failure to prevent it on a great scale.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: One of the forms of the ethnic cleansing which you also mentioned was to bring children of the perpetrators' ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Which, in another way, is to change the ethnic character of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could that be the result of individual cases or, through your enquiry, it was a systematic policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess both. The Commission did not have enough information to verify, let us say, these testimonies, who spoke in these terms. I guess it is possible that both happened. There are indications that it was commanded or that it was planned to do this, and it is important in regard to the chain of -- now I have to say it in Dutch -- [In translation]: It has do with the fact with the line of inheritance, heritage.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I did not get it. Is there translation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is translation. It has to do with the descendency, with the succession. As far as we could see, it meant that producing a child of another ethnic background was an automatic result of the fact that the child would have the ethnic origin of the father.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was there also male rape or was it mainly addressed towards the females?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, both are reported, but especially the female rape cases are a big number. You can see that there are more female victims caused by the detention camps that were specially for women. So there were two sorts of, two kinds of, two types of detention camps especially for women and there were a lot of rape cases reported. But there were also men who were raped and men were a victim of very serious sexual violence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before I go to the Prosecutor, I would like to ask you two or three questions: you were not there on the site yourself, were you, not in the case of the rapes; is that correct? Were you actually there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. As I am preparing my question, I wanted to be quite sure you were not on the site to carry out the investigations yourself. Were you actually there carrying out the investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not there. I was present at part of the investigation that was held by the Commission in Zagreb and I was present at several testimonies, testimonies also from the rape cases, but I did not do it myself. So I was there only -- my task there was only, let us say, to protect the rules that the Commission made before and to see if all things were OK and to represent the Commission in Zagreb and in Split.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the clarification I wanted, so now I can ask you my question. When you were drafting the Report you said you heard testimonies, so you discussed with your colleagues from the Commission. What was the general feeling, the general impression, which you had? What is your impression? Was this the major problem of the war in former Yugoslavia? Was the sexual aspect of ethnic cleansing, of rape, was that the overall principle element or was that one type of brutality amongst many others? What is your view, after having discussed it with your colleagues and having heard the testimonies? You do not have to tell us what was written in the Report, but what do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My own experience in hearing the victims was that they did not distinguish their own experience, their own wounds, the things that happened, as a special form of -- they saw it and they brought it within the whole violence and the violative conduct of the other party. So they did not distinguish itself, and they did not want to distinguish it because they did not want to hide their own experience in relation to the other violative acts and the other victims. So that is my experience in my own contact with victims. The Commissioned considered the sexual assaults and rape problem as a big problem and maybe, therefore -- the reason for considering it in this way was, of course, that there was a high public interest in what happened there, and all the world was looking to these publications on the rape cases. So that was one of the meaning factors that the Commission gave priority to this team, to this subject. It is in relation to other violation that happened, the killings, the murder, the torture, all kinds of these, I think the rape cases are not less but have the same character of violence as the others, as the other things like torture and killing, and that is the same as I had -- as the experience was of the victims. So it is one of all these things that happened to them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a second question, Professor: did you or your Commission at one point of time during your work see any protests that were made by the religious authorities or the medical authorities or any moral centres, intellectuals, writers? Was there any discussion? Do you have a feeling that someone, a religion or some moral authorities, expressed themselves on this particular point of the conflict whilst the conflict was going on for the many years whilst it was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many groups and also many institutes give us reports of their own investigation to what happened on the sexual assault and sexual violation and they expressed their -- I will go further in Dutch -- [In translation]: A lot of organisations and also a lot of victims contacted the organisations and they informed the Commission about their concern and about their dismay about what was going on. A lot of organisations were active to give a lot of publicity to the sexual violence that was occurring and, in particular, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a lot of organisations there took care of the victims, an important part of the victims, in so far as they were prepared to make known that they were a victim, they were taken care of by religious organisations. Those organisations informed the Committee and that was about the testimonies that they had given to these religious organisations.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I understand. Sorry, I want to stress my question, in Serbia, from the Serbian side, was there any protest? Was it said, for example, that from bishops or from the major religions or writers, did they talk about the problem of rape? You might have political ideas or political structures for one's country, but that was not my question. What I want to know, I want to know about the rape element. Did your Commission have any voice or opinion expressed from a health authority, a moral authority, that said to you, "This is not possible" or did you not have any such a statement made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Surely, you mean from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No translation of answer was audible)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, could you start again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, on the part of the Serbs, we did not get any response. Not to my knowledge, there was any response that the information published, that there would not be correct or that they would oppose this or that they would try to prevent this in the future. The only thing that was clear, that on account of the large publicity between April 1992 and December 1992, the number of notifications of rape and sexual violence was decreasing, and that was the reason for the Committee to assume that this publicity, apparently, had effect and even had an effect on these commands and orders.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All I want to say is that the Tribunal included in its decision that, if you wish, you may submit all reports, all written documents, which you think are good and which would support your statements.

utterances.speaker: MISS CLEIREN
utterances.text: I would appreciate to hand over some documents, part of which you have already. I will give you first the Annex of the Commission's Report of rape and sexual assault, a legal study, and I will also hand over some reports of other organisations made for the United Nations on the subject of rape. So do you want that I give the precise definition or can I hand it over?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is it a long list?

utterances.speaker: MISS CLEIREN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then do go ahead. Please list them so that we can decide what we should do it with.

utterances.speaker: MISS CLEIREN
utterances.text: OK. I will hand over the part of the Annexes of the Final Report of the Commission of Experts, Annex 2, Rape and Sexual Assault, a legal study. The second is a Report for the Security Council from the Mission of Dame Ann Warburton. It was a Commission for the European Community and it gives also a view of the situation in the former Yugoslavia. Then I will hand a part of the Report of the Commission on Human Rights on the question of violation of human rights and fundamental freedoms, of rape and abuse of women in the territory of -- sorry, I hear something I cannot understand. OK, sorry. I will hand over the Annex of the Report of the situation on human rights in the territory of the Former Yugoslavia by Mazowiecki. Then I will last hand over the article I wrote in the Criminal Law Forum on the subject of the applicability of Articles of the Statute. So that is all that I guess it can be useful for you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I look towards my fellow Judges. The Registrar, would you like to take the documents from the amicus curiae and include them in the files of the Tribunal? Mrs. Cleiren, I now will see whether the Prosecuting counsel has any questions that they wish to put to you. Are there any further questions which you think might be useful to put to the amicus curiae.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The Prosecution has been listening with the greatest interest to the statement of Professor Cleiren. We thank her very much for what we have heard from her. We have no questions. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Having heard that, we would like to thank you for having come here at our invitation. We now think that your hearing is completed. So, could you perhaps accompany Mrs. Cleiren and we will move on to the next witness? (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We now would like to call our next witness and that is Miss Irma Oosterman, one of our investigators. MISS IRMA OOSTERMAN, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will you put on your headphones, please? Do you hear me, Madam? You are going to read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Madam, will you take a seat? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you please state your name and maybe also spell it for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name Irma Oosterman, that is, I-R-M-A O-O-S-T-E-R-M-A-N.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What is your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this moment I work for the sexual assault in the war Tribunal. Before that I worked for the Foca investigation. I was also involved for the Prijedor investigation and for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. Your Honour, the evidence you are now going to hear will focus on the use of sexual assault as a degrading treatment during the time covered by this indictment. The use of that measure has been incorporated in the indictment charged as Grave Breaches and Violations of Laws and Customs of War and as Crimes Against Humanity. Before I ask you to tell us about your findings, I will ask you what did you do previously to come to our Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked for 14 years as police officer in the Netherlands. Before I joined the Tribunal I was a general investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you have also cases involving sexual assaults?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: To what extent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not a part of the vice squad, but I did some interviews of women who were raped and were sexually assaulted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: As a member of a team investigating these things, would you like to tell the court if you have in this office where you work a special team dealing with these questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we have a special team, the sexual assault team. We investigate the sexual assault and rape happened in former Yugoslavia and now we are focused on Bosnia, the eastern and northern side in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many members have you on that team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have nine members in the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could you tell the court approximately how many witnesses you and your team have interviewed concerning sexual assaults during this period you have been working on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My team is several hundreds, myself about 50. I spoke with more women and men, but not everyone is willing to testify in court or give a real statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: But you have been interviewing at least 50 persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Are we talking about victims now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are talking about victims now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could you tell us about where in the former Yugoslavia you have been or the areas you have been covering in your investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several areas in the northern and eastern part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you name any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can name, of course, Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Is that a town or is it a municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A municipality, Foca. For the rest, I am sorry I cannot talk about that because that is still ongoing investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I see, but can you mention some of the camps where you have been investigating things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can mention, of course, Omarska camp from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Foca High School, the Partizam sports hall and Bukb Ijlea from the Foca area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. When you use the term "sexual assault", can you please explain what you mean by that term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By that I mean rape, I mean other kinds of sexual assault, like men who were forced to perform fellatio on each other; women who had to do that kind of things, the fellatio, oral sex, and then people were forced to strip naked and went through all that kind of humiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So it is not only rape but there are different kinds of behaviour connected with the sex of the person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you try to describe for us what kind of people did commit this kind of crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The victims we spoke with were raped by soldiers and guards of camps, and sometimes even the commanders of the camps and even the Chief of Police of a special area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did it also happen that other peoples than those who belonged to the camp or who were managing the camp, did these kind of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were also men dressed in uniform, most of the time from paramilitary groups, who had access into the camps and came to take women away or rape them in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So people who had, in principle, nothing to do with the camps were invited to the camp by the commander to have a free access there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess so because all the witnesses tell that the commanders knew about it. They saw women taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So you have had statements when women say that other people than the people who belonged to the management did come in and did take them away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that happened often.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You mentioned the Foca area. Is there any evidence of sexual assaults of women occurring in detention camps in the Foca area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we have a lot of evidence there. We had, for example, the Foca High School and the Partizan sports hall where many women, children and elderly people were detained in and soldiers, guards and other people from paramilitary groups came in and took women out or sometimes raped them in the school building themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were there other patterns also? Did they take people out to stay for some period of length outside in other houses than the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they also took women out to other houses, sometimes even younger children, girls, 13, 14 years, were taken out. In the Foca investigation, we have one house where many women, young girls and children were taken to and were held there as if it was a kind of brothel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: OK. Were there many such brothels or houses outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK, if we talk about Foca, then I can say that there was one we really investigated, of course, there were other houses where women and children were held for a couple of days as well, and they had to obey all the orders. So they were rapes, sexual assault and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You mentioned the time, a couple of days, were there other longer periods than a couple of days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we talk about the real detention camps, then it is a month, two months, sometimes even longer. If I talk about the houses, then it varies, sometimes two days, sometimes 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What kind of people did commit these crimes in Foca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Foca, it was also guards from the camps, soldiers, policemen and the Chief of Police was involved in it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The camp commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The camp commander was, in fact, the Partizan sport hall was also the Chief of Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So people in this position did also themselves commit sexual assault or rapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and commanders of paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Have you been aware or been involved in investigations regarding events pertaining to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have in-house information that women were taken out during the fall of Srebrenica when the convoy was moving, but so far we did not investigate this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Are there ongoing investigations of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What about Sarajevo? Do you have any information what happened in Sarajevo of this type of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Recently, we got access outside Sarajevo in the Serb-held territory; there is a hotel and a restaurant where women were held in, but so far our investigation is not focused on it, but of course we will ongo that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am quite aware of the fact that you are involved in the investigations, you cannot give names, places, dates and things like that because these things have not yet been indicted. Nevertheless, I will ask you if you can say something in general about these investigations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general, I can say that you can see a pattern all over, women, men were separated. Women, children and the elderly people were taken to other separate places where men were taken, and then the soldiers and guards started to take women out and rape them, sexual assaulted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This is a kind of pattern, of course, but could you elaborate a bit on this kind of pattern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, especially the soldiers told often that they were forced to do it. They did not say who forced them to do it, but they were ordered do it. They also told -----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: By their superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but I mean they did not say names, and that they wanted to make Serb or Chetnik babies. The pattern was, yes, all over the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So there are statements of victims saying that the people who raped them were ordered to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Are there also, to your knowledge, people you have investigated who said they were not raped, but they were asked by the soldiers to tell other people that they were raped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We interviewed a couple of victims who told they were taken out to a separate place, then the soldiers told them, "Tell the others that we rape you", but in fact they did not. So -----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What kind of conclusion do you draw from that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conclusion is that there was an order that the soldiers had to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Have you found any evidence that commanders or the hierarchy of those detention facilities that you have mentioned knew about these sexual assaults?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already told you about Foca, for example, the chief of police knew about it. A couple of women went to him, complained about it but, nevertheless, he was one of the people who raped women himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge if this information did go even higher up in the hierarchy to the commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no information about it, but because all the witnesses tell that all the commanders or the chief of police were aware of the fact what happened, and I think it is a kind of general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Are there any statements about actions by paramilitary personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were also involved in this issue. In Foca, there was one house where women, young girls from 13 years old and older, were held and the Commander of this house was the Commander of paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you in your investigation also encounter rape directed against the male population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we have several statements taken from men who were forced to do fellatio on each other, even sons and fathers were forced to do so and men were forced to put objects in each other's anus.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Also, are there some statements of mutilation of the male genitals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were; we have one statement that one had to bite off the penis of another man. He did not manage and then soldier came and cut off a part of the penis and another one had to eat that part of the penis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you tell us something in general about the victims, what ages, what kind of people or something special about the victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the women we spoke with are civilians, the ages are from 13 years about till even 60. Of course, we found out that the more younger, attractive women were taken out more to be raped, but other women as well -- all kinds of education, all kinds of different backgrounds, but all were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Ages also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ages, yes, from 13 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This goes for men and women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Men are a little bit older, I did not find younger boys, but what was with the women was, of course, also that the younger girls were often still victims -- I am sorry, virgin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you tell the court something about the demeanour of your victims when you took statements from them? Tell us something about their willingness or unwillingness to give statements or to appear as witnesses maybe before this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, it is very difficult for those women to talk with. Most of the time it is the first time that they tell what happened with them. Husband does not know, children do not know. So every time we must spend a great -- a long time with those women. They are very afraid to appear here in court, just sit here, television, everything around. Most of them asked for anonymity and sometimes even they do not want to come because they are so afraid and so ashamed what happened with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you give us some percentage of willingness and unwillingness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is very difficult, but if I say I have 50 statements, maybe I spoke with 100 women, so maybe it is half and half who are willing to come. But the 50 statements we took, or I took, most of them asked for anonymity because they do not want to sit here in court and everyone facing perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could you say something about the widespread type of activities? Is this something that goes for all the part of Serb-held Bosnia or is it just in some few places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The areas we investigated is the pattern all over, the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many areas? Could you number the areas you have been involved in, all your team been involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven, eight areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Out of how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Out of how many areas?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: OK, as we maintain that this is a widespread way of acting, then we are, of course, interested in if it covers the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Is that, in your opinion, so, that this kind of activity covers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It covers the area of the northern and eastern part of Bosnia, and there we can see the pattern all over the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I see. You said something about the general knowledge of it. Have you heard somebody in your people you have been taking statements from saying, directly or indirectly, that these things are brought to the knowledge of the two people we have indicted in this special case, namely, Karadzic and Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not interview people who told that they told them, but because the commanders and the chief of police, they were aware of what happened, because they went to complain, the commanders and the chief saw what was happening, so that is why I think it is general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: It is general knowledge, in your opinion. Is there anything you would like to add without me asking you specifically about it? Is there something from the point of view of generality or widespreadness or specifics, patterns and things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK, for me it is very important to know in what kind of state all those victims are, because you must not forget that all those women, most of them, the men are already killed or still imprisoned or still missing, they do not want to know that the children, the family, the neighbours knows what happened with them. So, for them it is very important to have anonymity, to come in court. Those women were Muslim women. During the rapes the perpetrators were referring to that, even forced to them to eat meat, drink alcohol. Those things are very important for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did witnesses or victims you have been interviewing in Bosnia, are these the greater part of it or have you been even interviewing witnesses living today in another part of the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also interviewed people who are living in other parts of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So that is to be understood that there are many witnesses living in other parts of the world than in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Is the willingness of people living elsewhere greater to come to give evidence here than the other ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that it is greater. I mean, still for those people it is very difficult to talk about what happened with them. They feel very ashamed. So I do not see a big difference between that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, considering the ongoing investigations and the impossibility for us to go into direct details of names and places and things like that, I hereby conclude my questioning of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course without endangering any ongoing investigation and victims or witnesses, did you personally interview rape victims in and around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not interview a witness, a victim from the Srebrenica area. I think one of our members of the team interviewed one person who was taken out of the convoy and was raped, but because of the ongoing investigation I cannot offer any ----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Can you describe to the court what different problems women suffered due to the rape and sexual assault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you mean talking about the abortions, you mean that?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: No, about the general problems, psychological problems, emotional problems, harms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they have physical and emotional problems. Some are still strong because they want to survive and still live, and some do not want to live any more, but because they have children they go on with these kinds of things. Of course they have problems with vaginas and all kinds of anal problems. Some women had to give their children away, not their children but a child made by the Bosnian Serbs and some had to give abortion.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So, they suffer both, physical and psychological damage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In addition to that, could you describe or tell to the Court if women were also being beaten and killed in those detention camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have interviewed people who saw that women were killed as well. The women who were raped were threatened with guns, knives, sometimes they made scratches on their bodies with knives, put a cigarette butt on, that was during the rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Miss Oosterman, you mentioned that in cases of rape those who committed it admitted they had received orders, and sometimes orders, as you said, to make Chetnik babies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was the procedure which was used and was it similar in all the cases you have viewed? How did they manage to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like I have already told you, for example, women were taken out of the camp, were taken to another house or another building, soldiers ordered then to wash themselves, to clean themselves, then they came back in the room or wherever they were, then they said, "I am going to rape you and I will make you a Chetnik or Serb baby".

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where were they kept when they had the baby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
