utterances.text: Were they kept in detention until they had the baby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received information that that happened with women as well. So I did not interview someone, but we spoke with orphan houses, NTOs, and we know there were babies born as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: This method was adopted, was applied in several cases which you examined in several places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The same method?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same method.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The same method, I mean they all presented that they had high orders from the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said they received orders.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: They said they received orders. What happened to these women after they had the baby or what happened mainly to the women who were raped? Were many of them killed afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Many of them, of course there were many killed as well, but there are still many alive but what I already told you, there are very emotional and physical problems.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What happened to the whole family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends. It is various. Sometimes a husband does not live any more; sometimes they saw other children were killed. It is all different. I cannot say it is like this.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I mean, usually they had to leave their place of residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, yes, they had to leave and went to the so-called free territory.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You mentioned also there were assaults against men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Like forcing a man to eat the genital organs and castration. Was it a rather customary way of doing it or was it individual cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that it was, that this happened so often. We received information, we spoke with witnesses and victims who were there. There was one particular case where many men were held and they were forced to do that with each other. I am not talking about the cutting of the penis but fellatio and oral sex.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So there were males raped too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were men raped in so far as not the soldiers raped them, but they forced or ordered the detainees to do that with each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have one question in particular. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Fine. Were there any doctors in these camps, Serb doctors in particular? So were there any doctors and did you hear anything about the reactions they might have had seeing what was going on? I think everybody knows what was going on with regard to the mutilations. Were there any reactions on the part of the doctors? Did you hear that from anybody? Did anybody tell you or anybody saw it or was there no medical attention at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke with some witnesses who went to the hospital. I cannot tell more about which hospital, where it was, but the doctors they spoke with most of the time were not interested in those women. Those were the Bosnian Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The court has no further questions. The Tribunal would like to thank you for your testimony. I think we can leave it at that. The Registry or the Prosecution can perhaps show Miss Oosterman out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecution, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, our next witness, Dr. Colin Kaiser, will be testifying on the destruction of cultural and sacral sights. We have several visual displays we would like to set up in the courtroom. If there is an appropriate place for lunch, this might be a good time to do that so we do not waste any time setting up the displays.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel, we are not running late or anything. Let me have a quick look at my colleagues for action. We are going to adjourn this session and resume at 2.30 this afternoon. The session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (12.40 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment). (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Counsel for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, your Honours. As its next witness, the Prosecution calls Dr. Colin Kaiser to the stand. MR. COLIN KAISER, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you hear me? Can you hear, Mr. Kaiser?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will you read the oath that is in front of you, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Dr. Kaiser, the indictment within the procedure of Rule 61 of the case against Karadzic and Mladic, the Prosecution wanted you to appear here as a witness. So could you introduce -- you have the floor, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, would you please state your full name and spell it for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Colin Reid Erlin Kaiser. C-O-L-I-N R-E-I-D E-R-L-I-N K-A-I-S-E-R.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, each of you has been provided with a binder for this particular witness with the various photographs that he will be discussing, but we also have an updated evidence exhibit list for you with a smaller version of the map that is at Dr. Kaiser's side and transcripts of an audio radio tape that we also intend to play. So if I could present these to the usher to provide the court for inclusion in their binders? (To the witness): Dr. Kaiser, could you please begin by telling the court about your academic background and the variety of work that you have done concerning cultural and sacral sites, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By training and education, I am a Social and Institutional Historian, a graduate of the University of London. I have worked for the International Council on Monuments and Sites which is a non-governmental organisation that works very closely with UNESCO. I worked with them for six years and I was three years the Director of the International Secretariat. In November 1991, I was asked by the Director General of UNESCO to go to Dubrovnik as one of two observers for The Hague Convention and the World Heritage Convention. I continued to work with UNESCO on the question of Dubrovnik for several months. Toward the end of 1992, I began working with the Committee on Culture and Education of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, on the Council of Europe, yes, on the question of war damage to cultural heritage in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. I went on Missions for the parliamentary Assembly in November/December 1992. In March 1994, in June 1995, in October 1993, I worked for the Commission of Experts in Dubrovnik which was preparing the work for this Tribunal. In October 1994, I went back to work for UNESCO as a consultant in Mostar on the cultural heritage and I worked there in three long missions, each about six weeks and two months, until the summer of 1995. In October 1995, UNESCO asked me to go to Sarajevo to be its representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina. My recent work is not specifically cultural heritage; it involves all the fields of UNESCO's activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. During the course of your work with the cultural and sacral heritage in the former Yugoslavia, have you had occasion to write any reports or articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have contributed to eight information reports of the Parliamentary Assembly on destruction of cultural heritage in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have contributed to the Report of the Commission of Experts 1993. For UNESCO I have written reports specifically on Mostar. The Council of Europe Reports are public documents. The Reports of UNESCO are much more of a confidential institutional sort of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your work, have you had occasions to read and study various reports and publications about the status of the cultural and sacral heritage in the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read a certain amount of material about the cultural heritage, much of it rather general. However, in my work for the Parliamentary Assembly, for UNESCO, I have had access to a lot of documents that are mainly lists of cultural heritage, and a certain number of documents that are generally reports. The reports are of some interest. The reports began to come out in 1993. There are four reports I would like to mention. There was one report prepared by the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Historical and Natural Heritage of Serbia, which was about the destruction of sacral heritage in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. This document dates from January 1993. The report of Slobodan Mileusinic called "Spiritual Genocide" written in 1994 which is about the destruction of Serbian Orthodox heritage in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina over the period 1991/1993. In September 1993, the Republic Institute for the Protection of Cultural, Historical and Natural Heritage of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo produced an information document. A recent report, which is extremely important, was produced by the Institute for the Protection of Cultural, Historical and Natural Heritage of Bosnia-Herzegovina based in Sarajevo. This report, the first version of it, was written in September 1995 and has an annex, April 1996. These documents are -- the lists are, of course, what lists are; the lists are not very accurate. They are from the early part of the war. The other documents are extremely incomplete. The Serbian documents deal specifically with a certain type of heritage which is Orthodox heritage. The last two documents which I mentioned are of great interest because they attempted to give a larger view of the destruction of cultural heritage in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is the cultural heritage of everybody. The document that was compiled in September 1993, of course, has a problem because it was compiled under difficult circumstances. There was little access available by the people of Sarajevo to territory outside. The report of September 1995 is a different document. It has more documentation. It is more of an overview than earlier documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned previously the Council of Europe reports. Could you just take a minute and describe for the court what those reports were and how widely they were circulated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Council of Europe in 1992 began asking a lot of questions about what was going on to the cultural heritage in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was not a topic which generated a great deal of interest in the press. The press was interested in such isolated incidents, important incidents, as the burning of the National University library in Sarajevo and the Oriental Institute also in Sarajevo. But, generally speaking, we did not know very much about what was going on. So, this initial purpose was to try to find this information with the intention that, perhaps, if enough information were available, the International Community would pick up on it and would perhaps pressure local authorities into minimising the destruction of the cultural heritage. It was aimed at the International Conservation Community in the hope that it could intervene, that international agencies could intervene, to carry out protective works in cultural heritage where it was possible to do so. So these were the basic purpose, and we were also hoping that there would be a little bit more active intervention in the field. The machinery of The Hague Convention was not functioning at all. Although we live in a global village with an age of wonderful information and everything, it was extraordinary what we did not know. One of the successes of the reports was to stimulate monitoring of cultural heritage in Bosnia and also in Croatia by the European Community Monitoring Mission. I helped set up this system myself in 1994. It worked mainly with respect to sacral buildings, sacral heritage, it and it has worked a little bit fitfully. The ECMM now has a very heavy mission in Bosnia helping OSCE, and it has neglected its monitoring cultural heritage in the past few months. I would just say that this is a very frustrating activity in its earlier stages because in the earlier stages if you could not be on mission, you were collating a lot of reports; you were submitting them to a kind of critique de texte, comparing them, and it was often a futile exercise. What was very important was, in fact, the field visits which has permitted us to check the reports and permitted us to go and look at things that were not mentioned in the reports. Yes, you asked about the distribution. Well, these are public documents; in other words, the Council of Europe distributed them everywhere. They were distributed to Cultural Heritage authorities in Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were also given to the Serbian representative in Strasbourg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could just take a few minutes and please give the court a general overview of the cultural and sacral heritage that existed in the Bosnian Herzegovina region before the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think everybody has to bear in mind that Bosnia-Herzegovina is on a cross-roads, it is a north/south cross-roads between Central Europe and the Mediterranean world, and it is also on what is often called a fault line between civilisations, between Christendom in the west and Islam in the east. This is a country that has an extraordinarily rich cultural heritage. I will speak mainly about immovable cultural heritage and not about movables. With respect to the movables though, we can find enormous numbers of Neolithic, Paleolithic Iron Age, Bronze Age sites all over the country. The traces of the Roman occupation are also extremely numerous, for example, the famous site in Mogorjelo in the Neretva Valley but also in Hadzici -- no, Ilidza in Sarajevo. There are remnants, vestiges, of the early Christian Byzantine and Romanesque periods. There are early Slavic hilltop settlements, houses. There is the famous Bogomil culture, the Medieval culture, so-called; the Bosnian church as well which has left the famous stecci which are large blocks of stones, tombstones, all over the country. It is worth pointing out that this is a kind of bedrock of the cultural heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is something which is shared commonly by everybody in the country. Although there are accusations that archeological sites are misused by tanks and artillery, this has really had to be checked, but by and large, from my own work, I have seen that this heritage is not so badly damaged. The problem comes with the 15th and 16th centuries. There is the Ottoman conquest in the 15th and 16th centuries, and this changed extraordinarily the landscape of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then you had mosques, Mesjids which are mosques without minarets, medresas, mektebs, hamams, fountains, Turkish style houses. In the cities, in the villages, you have mahala districts. One can say that the Turks brought with them a very specific form of urban civilisation which has always marked the Bosnian towns and cities throughout its history. At the same time there was the disappearance or rarification, perhaps, of Christian churches and monasteries, some of which were destroyed, some of which deteriorated. In the 19th century there was a loosening up of the Empire, the Empire, of course, in its declining phase, and one finds more, I should say, western influences in terms of architecture. This was the period in which we began to find Orthodox churches being built, new Orthodox churches, new Catholic churches. The Austrian occupation in 1878 bought about another revolution, because we can see today the impact of Austrian town planning on such cities as Sarajevo, Mostar and Banja Luka; architectural styles and historicism, universities, libraries, municipal buildings, theatres. This was also the great period of church building, of Orthodox and Catholic church building. In fact, the Franciscan establishments that are all over Bosnia-Herzegovina have their present aspect from this period. By the 20th century, one could say that Bosnia was totally integrated into European vision of architecture and town planning. Up until World War II, however, you would find the sort of typical, vernacular, domestic architecture in the countryside. Being on a cross-roads, there is a tremendous amount of mutual influence. For example, the mosques, the great mosques of the 16th century, and even later, were built by Christian Herzegovinian stonemasons. It is a common tradition that it was Dubrovnik stonemasons that actually built the Old Bridge at Mostar. The Vucjakovica mosque in Mostar has Gothic traces. So there is this type of intermingling. The Austrians brought with them a pseudo-Moorish style, which was there own homage to the eastern ambience which they found. This style was in turn taken by local architects and adapted, which was what they did with art nouveau styles. So you find this tremendous interchange and sort of mutual influence. In terms of the common use and common respect of heritage, it is extremely interesting to point out that the Bogomil tombstones, nobody is really sure who is under them, but there is a feeling that it is not just Catholics, it is also Orthodox and Muslims. If we take such a famous pilgrimage site as the Church of St. John in Podmiljacja near Jajce, we find that this was a great healing site and people from all confessions came to this site. In Sarajevo itself, there is a pilgrimage which is taken from the Orthodox cathedral to St. Anthony's Catholic Church to the Turkish period Mausoleum of the Seven Brothers. People will make this pilgrimage and they will offer gifts at each shrine. In other words, you find this kind of mutual appreciation and sometimes this has strange echoes during the war. When I was in Olovo, in central Bosnia, there is a Franciscan church which was one of the major Catholic pilgrimage sites in Yugoslavia. This church had no damage at all. The Bosnian Serbian army which was very nearby and, in fact, these were local people, they would not attack this church. However, the mosque which was 200 metres down the hill had a whole number of artillery impacts in it. So this is kind of testimony to what Bosnia was, in fact, before the war. One thing that should be pointed out is that the war has tended to ethnosize cultural heritage which, in fact, was not ethnosized in the past. Perhaps the people who destroyed the Old Bridge at Mostar thought they were destroying Muslim cultural heritage. Certainly, the reactions to the destruction of the bridge were, "They are destroying our heritage, our Muslim heritage", but in fact the Old Bridge was something that was held in common by Serbs, Croats and Muslims. This must be kept in mind when considering all types of heritage, including things which are now considered only to be sacral objects of one faith. They were often, in fact, objects that were shared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you just detail the current status of efforts to develop a complete picture of the damage to the cultural and sacral sites in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry to have to say that the current status of these efforts is that they really are about zero. There is no co-operation between the entities, and there is no co-operation at the present time even inside the federation. Also, it should be pointed out the international community is not doing this job either. I regret this very much because there are a lot of myths that grew up around the destruction of cultural heritage, and these myths may end up becoming founding myths for new hatreds and a new war. I think some sort of international commission should, in fact, help to draw up an inventory to try to determine to a degree, not in a penal sense, but what the causes are and who are the responsible agents for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. At this time we would like to draw up on the screen Exhibit 161, which is 6/15. That will be on the computer screen. It is a smaller version of the larger map to the left of Dr. Kaiser. Dr. Kaiser, using this map, we would ask you to just give a general summary of the overall nature and extent of the damage to Bosnia and Herzegovina's cultural and sacral sites.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think I would like to refer, perhaps, to some figures before I comment the map -- is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Absolutely fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the last report that was prepared by the Institution for the Protection of Cultural, Historical and Natural Heritage in September 1995. The first thing to take into consideration is, well, first of all, this report has a lot of mistakes in it. I mean, the people who prepared it do not have access to western Herzegovina. They do not have access to the Republika Srpska. There are things like double counting; there are problems in presentation; there is a problem of mixing of all sorts of buildings in it. So it is not -- it is for from 100 per cent, you know, accurate, but it is an extremely interesting document. To address, first, the question of sacral buildings and the damage to sacral buildings, this report mentions that 1,183 mosques throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina have been damaged to some extent. I repeat "damaged"; they do not say "destroyed". Then 504 Catholics churches, 36 Orthodox churches and 5 Synagogues. So this gives a certain idea of the order of damage to sacral buildings. If you take a close look at the buildings that have been damaged and try to categorise them according to heritage, you get a somewhat different result. One thing I should point out is that in ex-Yugoslavia there was a fairly precise classification for cultural heritage. At the top level there was the so called zero monument. The zero monument was a monument of world class importance and in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was only one. It was the Old Bridge at Mostar; however, which was never on the UNESCO list, in spite of what has been said. Monument value (1) was a national monument; (2) was a regional monument and (3) was a local monument. It not always easy to distinguish between a (2) and a (3) and (1) and (2). But if we turn back to these figures that I have given you, the report indicates that of the 1,183 mosques, 190 of them were classified buildings. Of this some 500 churches, something like 48 of them, I believe, Catholic churches are classified; of the Orthodox churches, it is a smaller figure, it is only eight, and then two of the Synagogues were classified buildings. The report then goes on to note that 392 other historic buildings have been damaged to some extent. This gives us a total damage of about 640 listed historic buildings. Now, the inventory of classified buildings in Bosnia-Herzegovina runs up to 3,991. This means that, according to this Institute report, about 16 per cent of the listed cultural heritage has been damaged to some extent. It does not mean that 640 historic buildings are damaged in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. To keep in mind that the Bosnian register of monuments was woefully incomplete, but it is not the only country that has incomplete registers. There are some 61 town and rural ensembles complexes which are also classified, and we do not how many damaged buildings of historic interest there are here. We must consider there is a lot of vernacular architecture. Vernacular architecture may not be on anybody's list because it has been badly changed, but it is part and parcel of a cultural landscape. The truth of the matter is we do not know how many historical buildings have been damaged or destroyed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is not the 16 per cent that is indicated, it is not 640 but, to be honest with you, I cannot tell you how many there. To turn back to this map, I make an observation, it looks to me like this is a map of destruction which is imputed, in fact, to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that it is a probably a little bit conservative. There a certain number of municipalities in which there are no dots at all, Sokolac, Kalinovik, Sekovici, Lopare -- no, there are some in Brcko, Srbak and Laktasi, but I think the map gives a good idea of the range of destruction of mosques and churches in the territory of the Republika Srpska or else territory that was controlled by the Bosnian Army throughout most of the war. This map includes damage which can be imputed to military causes because some of the dots are on frontline areas, for example, Konjic. This is a front line area here. But a dot, for example, in Nevesinje, this is not front line area, this is behind the frontlines. The map does not give a good idea of the geographical range of destruction, that is, which could be attributed to Bosnian Serbian forces or other elements. I would like to know if I could refer to my notes, would it be possible ---

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- for some other figures?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, while you were referring to your notes, I would point out to the court that this particular map with the designations of the damaged mosques and the damaged Catholic churches is based on the investigations that the Office of the Prosecutor has undertaken. As Dr. Kaiser indicated, this is a very conservative representation at this point where we have been able to marshal the information and get a verification with which we are satisfied. So this is a very conservative estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would again refer to the report and I would refer to a particular type of damage which is mentioned in the report and this is damage by explosives. The report mentions, gives a category 4(B) which is destroyed by explosives. To be a little bit cautious, I take the category 4(B) and say that this is a building which is heavily damaged or destroyed by explosives. The report indicates that in the Republika Srpska, or else it was controlled by the Bosnian Serbian army, 161 mosques and mesjids were dynamited or destroyed by the use of tank mines, and 75 Catholic churches. I think that this figure is probably reasonably accurate within 10 per cent plus or 10 per cent minus. The buildings indicated fully 70 of the mosques, 70 were listed monuments and eight of the Catholics churches. If we were to take destruction by other elements, according to the use of explosives, for example, attributed to the HVO, the report indicates 12 mosques and two Orthodox churches and monasteries, especially in the Neretva Valley area. All of these buildings are, in fact, listed buildings. I think that this estimate for the HVO would be a little bit low. The report does not indicate any buildings destroyed by explosives in territory controlled by the armija, and I have never seen a building destroyed by explosives in the territory controlled by the army in my own missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: For clarification, when you refer to the "armija", is that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you give the court just then a general overview of the actual responsibility for the destruction of cultural and sacral sites in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, general overview in terms of?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In terms of the entities responsible, just a comparative breakdown, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that these figures about dynamiting, in fact, are fairly faithful in terms of who is responsible for most of the damage. I repeat that we do not know everything in the Republika Srpska, and we have to be very careful, we have to investigate the whole territory, but I think it is indeed correct to say that the Bosnian Serbian entity was responsible for much more damage and destruction of cultural heritage than the other entity or the two subentities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You personally have visited many of these sites of destruction, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you just briefly explain to the court the various ways one can determine the nature and the source of the damage found at these cultural and sacral sites?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to go in terms of least damage to most damage, in architectural terms, I mean, one first could point out that there is damage by pillaging and small arms fire. This is not so serious for the building but it can often be very serious for the contents of a building. Then the second type of -- of course, this is difficult to attribute this sort of damage. It can be kids throwing stones through windows and not necessarily a soldier shooting but somebody else shooting. Then there is artillery damage. Artillery damage is very easy to recognise. It is often easy to attribute, particularly in areas, in front areas that have remained stable for a long time. You simply look to see where the front is and where the enemy is. After a certain amount of experience with buildings, you can recognise the type of shell that it is. This type of damage from artillery, of course, is spectacular. It makes good film footage. But, in fact, there are very few buildings that are pummelled to the ground by artillery. There is, however, another type of damage that is associated with artillery and that is burning damage. That is usually much more serious. Burning damage can be done often by heavy mortars, a heavy mortar through the roof of a building into the attic can set a very nice fire. It is not always easy to attribute where the mortar is shot from, especially when the roof has gone and the internal structure of the building has gone. Then there is a question of burning damage by arson which is set by troops or set by unknown parties. Finally, the last type of damage is the resort to explosives which is by far the most serious type of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If we could direct the court to your trip to Mostar. I believe you took that trip in December 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your trip in December '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of the trip was that we did not really know much of what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina in terms of the cultural heritage and what was happening. Mostar is a very, very important town in terms of its heritage. It had been a scene of a battle and, despite the fact that it was liberated with relatively open access, we did not really know much about it. So the objective was to get to some site that was fairly easy of access. At this point you must keep in mind that this activity of looking at cultural heritage was not regarded by anybody as being very important, so it was very difficult to sort of wonder around central Bosnia; you could not get any help from any of the big agencies, UN agencies or others. So, I mean, this was handy in terms of a local vehicle to drive up the Neretva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was this first trip shortly after what we will refer to as the first battle of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was in December 1992. The first battle of Mostar ended in the mid part of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Who were the primary participants in the first battle of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, BSA, which had more or less completely surrounded the town through most of the battle, and local defence units and especially the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the court what you saw during your first mission to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw a great deal of artillery damage done to the town of Mostar which I attribute to the BSA because the BSA was much, much better armed than the HVO. There was a lot of damage from explosives. The BSA dynamited all the bridges in Mostar except for the Old Bridge -- a tremendous amount of burning damage. Most of the Austrian period buildings, in fact, which were burnt out in Mostar were, in fact, burned out in the first battle and not in the second battle. There was damage from explosives to the new Orthodox church in Mostar which was completely destroyed in the summer of 1992 as a reprisal, and there was a lot of reprisal damage in the Neretva Valley to villages inhabited by Serbs, to the monastery of Zitomislici, a 16th century monastery. So there was a tremendous amount of damage to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you arrive at any conclusions as a result of your observations in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was an extremely frightening experience. I had some experience of Croatia, and I had never seen anything so intensive and I had not yet seen this sort of cycle, initial damage and reprisal. It seemed to me at the time that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was rather more vicious, in fact, much more vicious than the war in Croatia, and that there was a great danger of really extensive and serious damage to the cultural heritage. Finally, the question came into my mind, in fact, well, maybe was this damage to cultural heritage, in fact, part of the strategy of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that just a bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the last part?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: The last statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I say, it is a question of my surprise. In Mostar, practically everything of cultural value had been hit, and it is extremely surprising to see Austrian buildings which do not particularly have any strategic value, and maybe they are not first class monuments, but they are part of a landscape deliberate burnt out and, of course, in this tremendous amount of damage to the mosques. But to see buildings, this first time I also saw sacral buildings that were dynamited. This is quite an extraordinary thing to see, particularly a venerable building like the monastery at Zitomislici. So I began to ask myself questions, I mean, what is going on here and what is going to happen? What is everybody up to in this part of the world?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: OK, thank you. At this time if we could have the lights dimmed, please, and we have a series of photographs showing some of the damage to Mostar at the hands of the Serb forces. This first photograph is Exhibit 162, 6/1. Could you describe this, please, Dr. Kaiser?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Sevri Hadji Hassan mosque which is listed as a monument of third level in Mostar. It is Donja Mahala, right near the Neretva River. This building was before 1620. On the left, where you see the roof of the red house, well, there was a minaret there and the minaret is totally destroyed. If you look at the facade, you can see a lot of damage which is, in fact, artillery damage done and this is done by the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. For reference, your Honours, this particular mosque is one of the ones named in the indictment. If we could have Exhibit 163 shown, please, Dr. Kaiser?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Franciscan Church of St. Peter and St. Paul. It was built in 1863. It was built at a period in which the Ottoman empire was sort of loosening up before the Austrian occupation. This was destroyed and burned by shelling in May 1992. It was done by the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Again, your Honours, this particular Franciscan church also appears in the indictment itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just maybe one other comment is that the church is totally destroyed, but to the right are the buildings of the monastery which received extremely little damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we can have Exhibit 164, please? Dr. Kaiser?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is entrance to the Catholic Bishop's Residence. This residence was built in 1906. It housed a library, the episcopate library, of 50,000 volumes and a library, a personal library of the Bishop of 10,000 volumes. It was destroyed, burnt out by shelling also in May 1992 by the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 165 shown, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Ibrahim Aga Saric mosque built in 1623. This is, in fact, a monument which is classified level (2). This is an example of mosque shooting, of minaret shooting, in fact. The minaret is cut from just below the gallery up and you can see the type of damage that part of the falling minaret can do. It has come down through the roof. This was also done by the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this particular mosque is referred to in the schedule that is part of the statement of facts that supports the indictment. If we could have Exhibit 166, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Karadjo Begova mosque built in 1557. This is a monument of national importance. You can see here that the pinnacle of the minaret is shot off at the level of the cerefa. What you cannot see is on the other side of the minaret there is a very, very big impact, an artillery impact, about a third of the way down. This damage was also done by the BSA in the summer of -- during the period of battle, the first battle of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, again this particular mosque is listed in the schedule underlying the indictment. Finally, if we could have Exhibit 167, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an interior shot of the Koski Mehmed Pasha mosque built in 1618/1619. It is a level (2) in terms of monument classification. You can see shots through the dome. You can also see an artillery impact down at the bottom of the picture. In addition, this mosque, its minaret is cut, completely cut, at the level of the drum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Again, your Honours, this particular mosque is listed in the schedule supporting the indictment. Dr. Kaiser, one cannot help but notice the damage to the minarets; do you attach any significance to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in Mostar there are 14 listed historic mosques and 12 of them were damaged in the first battle. Five of them have their minarets cut at one level or another. The remaining four have been hit on the minaret and usually high. You will see some from this picture. I have seen all over the country that often the minaret shooting is, in fact, rather high. It is at the gallery level. So, one is not entirely sure what the motivation of the shooting is. I mean, it could be alleged that this is an observation post that is being shot at, the same way that often it is alleged that the belfry of a church is being shot at. But, if you take a look at such cases as the Koski Mehmed Pasha Mosque, with the shots through the dome and on the drum of the dome, if you take a look at the Sevri Hadji mosque which has lost its minaret completely and has all these shots all over the southern facade, well, you find that there is a will, not just to bang away at a possible shooting post, but in fact to destroy a minaret completely and also to do significant structural damage to the mosque. The mosque minaret is a very characteristic sight in a Bosnian town. It is on the horizon. You can see the town sometimes for long ways away because of the minaret. The minaret means that this is a town which is inhabited by Muslims. It is a sign of the presence of Muslims. It is also the sign, an historic sign. It is a sign of the period of the Ottoman Empire which could be regarded, perhaps, by some parties as a period of occupation. So, the siting on a minaret, the targeting of a minaret, certainly does have a symbolic significance to it. It is trying to change this Bosnian town, to eliminate the memory. It can also often be taken as a kind of a warning. If you damage the minaret high, you do not shoot it down completely, you can see from far away also that the minaret has been damaged and that, perhaps, you are not wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now move to another trip that you took to Konjic-Olovo and other areas. I believe that trip was in June 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was in June. In March I made a trip which was in western Herzegovina, in Mostar. In June, I went to central Bosnia. The objective of this trip was the same thing as the objective of other trips, is that we did not have very much information about what had happened on the frontlines between the federation and the Republika Srpska. At the same time, we did not know very much really what happened in the pocket areas, that is, the areas that were affected by the war of 1993/1994 between the Croats and the Muslims. So again it was a fact-finding trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What did you see on this trip and what conclusions did you reach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you like me to give you my itinerary?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. Well, we visited, for example, Konjic here, Olovo, Kladanj -- I am first showing you the towns that are on the front line -- Kalesija, Tuzla, Gradacac, Gracanica, Zavidovici, Maglaj, Tesanj, Travnik. So these were the frontline areas and on the frontline areas include also villages in this area, on this part of the trip. Well, we saw a tremendous amount of artillery damage done by the Serbs. It was somewhat -- one has to be a little bit nuanced. It was said often that Travnik had been destroyed by the BSA and that Tesanj had been destroyed by the BSA and Kladanj had been destroyed by the BSA. Fortunately, one discovered, we discovered that in these towns there was, in fact, rather little damage from the artillery. On the other hand, we found such towns as Maglaj or Konjic, just to name two of them, or Gradacac, in particular, we found a lot of damage to cultural heritage, to sacral buildings and to sacral heritage. Then there was the other part of the trip which was, of course, in the pocket areas and the areas in which there had been a lot of fighting between the Muslims and the Croats; Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Vitez, Zepce was the Croatian pocket here. What could be observed in these areas was also a certain amount of resort to explosives by the HVO. Generally speaking, Orthodox churches in these areas were not touched very badly. They were often locked up. As I say, the question of the stone through the window, that sort of thing, and the territory of the armija, one would across from time to time an Orthodox or a Catholic church, particularly in a rural area, which would be burned. But, generally speaking, the churches in the towns were also carefully, well, in fact, guarded after a certain manner of speaking. So those would be the sort of general conclusions of the trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could have the lights lowered once again? We have several photos from this trip. First, if we could have Exhibit 168 brought up, please? I believe that is 6/7. Dr. Kaiser, would you describe what is shown here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is the Carsijska Mosque in Konjic. This is, apparently, not a listed monument -- I am a little bit surprised -- and this is an example of minaret shooting. You can see a shot very high at the gallery level and another one lower. It looks as if there was, perhaps, the beginning of an intention to do more damage to the minaret than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this particular mosque is actually named in the indictment. What entity would have been responsible for this shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would be the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 169, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Vardacka Mosque in Konjic. Well, the damage is obvious, it is high, it is to the pinnacle. You will see down below there at the right monitor is European Community Monitoring Mission staff, and they said that this damage and the damage to the preceding mosque was probably done by tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Is this mosque also damaged by the BSA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is done by the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, for a point of reference, this particular mosque is included in the schedule supporting the indictment. Now if we could have Exhibit 170, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an unnamed mosque, but it is a mosque of quality. You can see it is a stone mosque in Olovo. This is a mosque that is just 200 metres down the hill from the Franciscan church that I mentioned. You will see either an artillery or tank impact on the wall. If you look up to the left, you will see damage done to the roof and further up to the right also to the roof, and you also see that the post in the window has also been shot out. This was done by the BSA. Local people said it was done on one occasion in February '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Again, your Honours, this particular mosque is contained in the schedule supporting the indictment. Thank you. I would like to move to a trip that you took to Banja Luka recently. When did you have occasion to visit Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I visited it at the beginning of June of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit 171, 6/10, brought up on the screen, please? Dr. Kaiser, have you seen Exhibit 171 before? Have we shown this to you before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What does this represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is a rather schematic town plan of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What does it show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it shows mainly the centre area town, but what it shows mainly is the location of the mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Is there any significance to the concentration of the mosques shown on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is. I mean, this is in some ways the perimeter of the Turkish town. Banja Luka was conquered a bit late in 1528 by the Ottomans. It is in the north western part of Bosnia. It was of great strategic importance for them, so it was also extremely important for them to leave their mark. The foundation of these mosques is extremely symbolic of a regime, of a way of living, and so this accounts for this concentration of mosques in this particular area. I should also say that the Turks built a fortress, well, rather built on the ruins of a Christian fortress, they built a very big fortress. So this town, whole town, is a symbol of their power.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In referring to this map, could you describe to the court what parts of the city you are were able to visit on your trip to Banja Luka in June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we came in to the town from the south which is from the right. There is a road, you can see a little arrow there, and that is the road to Mrkonjic Grad and that is the main street. So we went completely up the main street following it as it sort of keeps going to the left, and then past up towards our hotel which was off the map to the north. I also on one occasion came back down the main road, and right practically in the centre of the map there is a bridge across a river. I crossed this bridge, took the right turn, right-hand turn there and continued down the road. That is really what I saw of this area that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In walking around the area last month in Banja Luka, did you notice any minarets in this general central area of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, minarets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If we could have the lights dimmed, please, and Exhibit 175, 6/13 brought up on the screen, please? Dr. Kaiser, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is, in fact, the one mosque I saw. This is the one on the other side of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Does this photograph accurately depict the way it looked last month when you visited there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could now have Exhibit 172, 6/11 brought up on the screen? For reference, this is a smaller version of the enlarged photograph that we have here in the courtroom. Dr. Kaiser, would you tell us a little bit about the mosque depicted in Exhibit 172, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the Ferhad Mosque. It was built in 1579 by the bey in Banja Luka whose name was Ferhad Pisa Sokolovic. He built it with a ransom money he received from giving back the Sana of a Christian captain who had been killed in a battle. This is an extremely important building. It is No. 1 on the classification. In fact, it is one of two buildings like this in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, why is it of a particular nature? Most mosques have simply a central plan, a central chamber which is square, rectangular. This one is rather different. It has, in fact, along both sides what could be considered to be naves. You will see right between, near the base of the minaret and the square central section, you will see a little bit of a trough roof and this indicates where the other nave is. Also, at the rear, at the south end of it, there is a semi-dome because we have a circular apse, we call a circular apse, where the main mihrab is. So we have three naves in this mosque. Under the stone pore where the other two naves are, we also have mihrabs at the right side and the left side. So this is a very, very -- in terms of the faithful, there is a lot of faithful who are going to be gathered here in this mosque, outside and inside. It is comparable to the Ghazi Husrev Bey mosque in Sarajevo. It has an extremely large minaret 41.5 metres high. You will see, in the foreground you will see one mausoleum. There, in fact, were three. Ferhad Pasa Sokolovic was, in fact, buried in one of the mausoleum and, apparently, standard burials were buried in one of the other ones. You can also see, not very well, but near the entrance on the left you will also see a fountain. So this was an extremely important and imposing building. When it was built, in fact (and it is thought that it was built by one of the students of Mimar Sinan who was one of the main Turkish architects working in Constantinople at the time), it is not just, it should not be, we should not limit the importance of this building and say this is an important sacral Islamic building; this is an important building in Banja Luka. This building was, perhaps, the symbol, the monument symbol, of this town. It was a reason for civic pride. You will find it in all guide books. You will find it on postcards. This is something that I believe all citizens of Banja Luka identified with and found reason for pride in the existence of this mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 174, 6/14, brought up, please? Your Honours, to demonstrate Dr. Kaiser's point, this is just a postcard from the area depicting this particular mosque. Dr. Kaiser, when you were in Banja Luka last month, did you see anything that looked like this particular mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If it had still been there would you have seen it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At this time if we could have Exhibit 173 brought up on the screen, that is 6/12? Again, this is a smaller version of the enlargement we have here in the courtroom. Your Honours, recently we had investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor go to these sites in Banja Luka when we were finally allowed some access to the area. This photograph which is, in fact, two photographs put together, both of those photos were taken by one of our investigators in late April. This, in fact, represents what is left of the mosque. It is now a vacant lot. There are some points of reference with the "before" and "after" photograph. The tall trees in the background, the one tall tree on the right, and the building in the rear that is still standing, those are two points of reference that you can compare with the "before" and "after" photographs. Dr. Kaiser, in your opinion, why would the Bosnian Serbs so thoroughly destroy a mosque of this nature and eliminate all traces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you want to get rid of all traces, or if you want to get rid of all Muslims in a particular area, and you assimilate mosques to Muslims, it is quite clear that you would go after this building, particularly because it is so important in terms of the image of the town. It seems rather logical that this would be part of the step of eliminating the Muslim presence and also eliminating a large part of the history of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Do you know what effect this destruction might have had on the local population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not had this discussion with the local people -- I hope to have it one day -- but I have had, but in similar discussions, for example, in Mostar one comes across, for example in Mostar west, there was a great deal of shock, regret and shame about the destruction of the Old Bridge. I think there was probably something akin to that reaction in Banja Luka. I would notice that there is still a photograph of the Ferhad Mosque in the museum in Banja Luka. It has not been removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At this time we would like to move to some other trips that you have taken. Recently, have you been able to travel through the areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina controlled by the BSA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about half a dozen times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When did you begin travelling in these areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first trips to Pale were in February and then in April we began moving a little bit more to other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Maybe you could take the pointer and the map and just generally show some of the areas that you have been able to visit recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one trip I took down to Gorazde, down through here, and this means that you have to cross through the Republika Srpska to go through Rogatica, notably; another trip down to Foca through Republika Srpska, and another trip up to Doboj here which is just inside the Republika Srpska; of course, the trip to Banja Luka here, and I have also been through part of the anvil area here, Mrkonjic Grad, and then up through Bosanski Petrovac, up to Bihac, and this area was also under the control of the Bosnian Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: I would briefly like to review some of the areas you have been to. You have been to Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Who currently controls Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Do you know if Donji Vakuf had any mosques or minarets before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had two mosques at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In your trip through Donji Vakuf, did you see any minarets or mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: All right. Similarly, you have been in Rogatica, as you have said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were there mosques and minarets in Rogatica before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were several mosques, including some listed buildings, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Rogatica is in the control of the BSA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When you went through Rogatica did you see any mosques or minarets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You have been to Foca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Is it the same situation there as far as mosques and minarets being present before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not examine the town completely, but I saw no mosques and I saw no minarets. Foca was very important because it had 10 mosques, all of them listed, including the great Ilidza Mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Foca is in BSA control as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Finally, with regard to Doboj, you have been through Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did Doboj before the war have mosques and minarets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were you able to see any mosques or minarets when you went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Throughout your entire travels in the area controlled by the accused Karadzic and the accused Mladic, have you seen any minarets at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1995, when I was based in Mostar, the early part of 1995, I visited Kupres which had just been taken back by the HVO. In Kupres there was a mosque, an unfinished mosque, and an unfinished minaret which were intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: That is the extent of the number of minarets that you have seen in your travels through Serb controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the only one I have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could take a moment for the court and describe to them the significance of this type of destruction of cultural and sacral sites in human terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would it be possible for me to look at my notes again on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, according to the information that we have, there seems to be to have been an attempt in the territory of the Republika Srpska to eliminate the Islamic sacral heritage. This corresponds to between 100 and 200 mosques that are classified of historic value. We do not know exactly still how many of them are destroyed, but we have a lot of fears about this. Those are buildings built in the 16th and 17th centuries. These are obvious and obviously an important part of the heritage of country, but they are not just a part of the heritage of the country; they are part of the European heritage. If you take with the exclusion of Spain, we are talking about the western most penetration of the Ottoman Empire. The buildings are important for the Bosnians and they are important for our history as well. I think their loss is, in fact, something that is irreplaceable. It would appear that there has been a similar tendency with respect to Catholic churches in this area. This usually represents a more modern heritage. One may have whatever judgement one wishes to have about the aesthetic value of historicist architecture from the period, but it is part and parcel of cultural heritage, 19th century churches. I should point out that there has often been a lot of damage done to Ottoman heritage in the Neretva Valley. This is serious as well, perhaps less serious in numerical terms. There has been damage also done to Orthodox heritage in the Neretva Valley. This is serious, but this is totally at a different dimension. What is the significance, though, of the destruction of the Islamic heritage and the Catholic heritage in this area? In the reports of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, we always talked about cultural cleansing alongside ethnic cleansing. In other words, you cannot simply ethnically cleanse a people and eliminate them entirely this way. The way of eliminating them also involved a destruction of their heritage. In other words, you are eliminating a sacral building and in this way you are eliminating the memory of having lived together. So I think this is one of the general importance of destruction of this type of heritage. If you turn to such other questions as the destruction and loss to civil, secular, cultural heritage, we would find that there has been an awful lot of damage in towns to buildings of all periods, to vernacular architecture, to houses. In the countryside, there has often been an awful lot of damage in ethnic cleansing and ethnic counter cleansing, also in central Bosnia. If you add up together these different types of damage, you come with a rather obvious conclusion. I mean, you have a kind of radical change in the physical environment in which people are living. This means that you are talking about the removal of the signposts of collective and individual life. In this sense, we are talking about a spiritual impoverishment for people all over the country. Remember, although we have this problem of the ethnic identification of cultural heritage, in fact, what you are doing is that the destruction of a mosque is a destruction of something within a Serb or something within a Croat as well. Destruction of an Orthodox church is a memory that a Croat has. You are dealing, breaking down the whole identity with the destruction of this cultural heritage. Now, much of what has been destroyed, let us say, dynamited and raised, well, in fact, hardly any of it will rise again, and much of what has, in fact, been heavily damaged in the war will be destroyed in the process of reconstruction. So we are talking about something which really is a catastrophe for the peoples on the spot. Now, there are two, perhaps, final questions that come to mine mind. The first is, is this type of destruction a precedent? Secondly, what does it represent for us? To answer the first question, I think one has to go back to the history of the region. I think that the Ottoman conquest was probably not as tender as some complacent historians had made it out to be. I think there was probably a lot of destruction carried out by the Turkish armies of cultural heritage, sacral buildings. It must be remembered that when the Austro-Hungarians reconquered the parts of Croatia which were under the control of the Turks, they virtually eliminated all sacral and secular buildings associated with the Ottoman rule. It should be remembered also that in World War II, the Ustashas did a tremendous amount of damage, an appalling amount of damage, to Orthodox heritage in Croatia and also in the diocese of Banja Luka. It should also be remembered that in 1945, after the war was over, for example, in Mostar there were six mosques, historic mosques, and mesjids that were pulled down; in Kladanj there were four. So, in this area there are precedents and there are memories of the destruction of cultural heritage. It has been done commonly in the past. So one could say that this is not being invented, it is not new, it did happen, but is there something new in it? There is, perhaps, a conjunction of removing peoples and removing the traces of peoples and carried out by states that knew all the rules. Remember that the military forces that have done this damage were very well versed in the laws of war. They all knew The Hague Convention. The civil authorities knew fully well the value of the heritage that was being destroyed on their territories and which, by their own laws, they were bound to protect. All of this was done in full view of an international community that was far better informed and more concerned than people in the 16th century or even in the 1940s. I think that we are in the presence of a kind of synthesis, synthesis of practices from the past with the efficiency of modern state and a 20th century sophistication in social engineering in reverse. The authorities fully understood the significance of heritage as one of the bonds that holds together a society, and particularly a society people who have differing traditions. I do not want to sound overdramatic or prophetic, but such combinations of brutality and sophistication strike me as a rather ominous challenge for the future. In all of our societies, there are movements, there are political parties, people and intellectuals who dream of cleaning their territory and cleaning their history, and the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina has shown how it can be done and that it can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At this time point, your Honours, we have a final exhibit and this would go towards notice and knowledge for the accused Karadzic. With your permission, we would play that?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 177 which is an audio tape played? This is a rebroadcast by the BBC, February 27th 1992 radio broadcast by Radio Sarajevo. We have translations. Hopefully, we can have this translated as it is being played. (The tape was played): (In translation): "In our conference today, I have received an announcement which says that yesterday at 11 o'clock, just shortly before midnight, a bomb fell on a significant cultural building of Banja Luka. This is the first time something like this has happened in our history. I fear that this is a type of revenge that is taking place. This is an attempt to provoke us, to provoke confrontation. We are not blaming the Serbian people for this attack of vandalism, but we are blaming the extremists. The Muslims must also contain themselves and must not react to it. "The sacral cultural heritage is something we hold very sacred. I condemn this act of vandalism and I do not think that the Serb people are responsible, but that fascists are responsible. I condemn all acts of such vandalism".

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: So, your Honours, we can see from this broadcast that as early as February 1992, the accused Karadzic was made aware of the risk that these sacral and cultural sites were at with the upcoming hostilities being planned at that very time. Finally, we would like to note for the court that we have had investigators in Srebrenica recently in connection with that investigation, and that the practice of this destruction of sacral and cultural sites continued on through July 1995. If we went to trial, we have photographs showing minarets and mosques in the Srebrenica area. When our investigators were there recently, there are no traces of minarets and these mosques have been destroyed. That concludes our presentation and we would now open it up to questions from the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I look towards my colleagues first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, I would like to thank you for your clear and most informative survey of the destruction of the cultural and spiritual heritage in Bosnia, in particular. Just to dispel any doubt concerning some of the very clear conclusions which we could reach listening to you, I would like you to tell me, could it have been possible that such damage would result from the exchange of fighting in any of these areas or it had to be a premeditated and well organised attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a difficult question to answer. It is not impossible that you can develop a dynamic of destruction as things go on, it is not necessarily premeditated, but I think that one can only draw a conclusion when one has looked at the total, the long calendar of the destruction of cultural heritage in the area, sacral heritage, I say a calendar, to follow it all the away across the territory. Perhaps this calendar will help the Tribunal to be able to sort out what the intentions were, but I could not personally say that this was definitely a premeditated plot.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Speaking of this calendar, you gave us a synthesis of the calendar by mentioning that 1,123 mosques were damaged, 504 Catholic, 36 Orthodox and five Synagogues. Judging by the percentage of the damaged, let us say, religious heritage, could you conclude that it was a strategy in all the war or, at least, in some of the factions had it as a strategy, judging by the number and the systematic way it was done ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it was -----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: -- and was it more due to the attitude of one of the parties in particular or a general systematic strategy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if it was not the strategy at the beginning of the war, it certainly became part of the strategy. You cannot possibly have 1,183 damaged mosques without something fairly deliberate being done. I return back to my original position; it certainly became one, it was very useful, but destruction or damaging of a minaret is clearly a sign to a population. I know of an example in western Herzegovina where you have a village which is totally undisturbed, with a village of Muslims in 1993, and then in 1994 or 1995 you have one shot on the minaret. This is a signal. Hitting a minaret is also one way of chasing, chasing the people. So, in fact, this can be actually integrated very carefully into the method. It can be part of the method.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: My first question goes to the Council for the Prosecution. Do you have all the reports which were mentioned at the beginning of the presentation of Dr. Kaiser?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We have these reports and they are very voluminous, so we have not presented them as exhibits, but if the court would like access to them, we absolutely can provide them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel for the Prosecution. I have taken note. I now turn to Dr. Kaiser. As regards the systematic character of the destruction that you mentioned, doctor, was there any damage to Muslim cemeteries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In translation): At the beginning of the war ... (No translation of answer was audible) It was -----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. I think there was a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Please continue in the language which is the easiest for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will continue like this otherwise it will be difficult for you. So what happened is in the visits, in my trips, I saw it was really a question of individuals who decided to shoot, but I never saw a cemetery which was bulldozed down. I never saw a site where I could have thought had been bulldozed. I could have imagined that in Mostar, for example, where you had the Vucjakovica mosque that was dynamited in 1993, now that mosque was surrounded by a cemetery that was used heavily during the war, unfortunately. Now, there were some tombstones which were damaged, but no-one disturbed that cemetery. That is something I find time and time again, and also in the Republika Srpska because you can recognise the Muslim cemeteries very easily.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. I also wanted to ask you whether during your investigations, even if this goes beyond our presentation, so in the visits you mentioned you also looked at the other monuments which are part and parcel of the heritage of a people, the universities, the libraries, etc., the administrative buildings, the courtrooms; could you very briefly give us some brief idea of whether those buildings were damaged so you could ruin the inheritance of a people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think I was concentrating now on the questions which you were putting to me as regards cultural heritage and sacral sites. But I do not want to minimise the importance of this destruction of the rest of the inheritance or heritage. I mentioned the town of Mostar, in particular, where I said the buildings during the Austrian period, the bars(?), the administrative buildings, the schools, etc., they were burnt during the battles there, and this type of building is an integral part of the town. For example, as I was saying the theatre, the bars, the schools, are something that are used daily and come up also in different towns where you found the history in the library, in the university, the national library of Sarajevo. It was not a Catholic or Muslim building, but it was part and parcel of the town. Everyone shared the services of the library, the Serbs the Croatians and the Muslims. During our trips there, we tried to focus on that heritage. You are absolutely right when you are saying there is not only the sacral heritage, there is also the heritage of everyday, of part and parcel of their life, and that is equally important. It is just as important as the rest. That heritage was heavily damaged. When I talk about buildings that will no longer be built up again, after the war you might think that some efforts are going to do for the churches and for the mosques, at least those who have not been too damaged, but for many other buildings in the civilian life, the damages that have been done to those buildings will probably end in their destruction, and they will depend entirely on the Austrian period which runs the serious risk of disappearing in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I would also like to ask you based on the figures you have given me that -- I will start again so that you can hear the beginning of my question. Based on the figures that you have given us, we have noticed that there was almost no synagogue, that there was no synagogue which was damaged. Could you give us an explanation as regards that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, there are not a lot of synagogues in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the synagogues in Sarajevo had minor damages, but there is one thing you should not forget, that when you look into Sarajevo, there was an enormous amount of damage done, particularly in the modern areas. There were some historical buildings who were heavily damaged, like the library I mentioned. You can think also of the Magribija Mosque which is in Marin Dvor which has lost its minaret. There are lots of minor damages and destruction done to the churches, to the mosques as well. But one thing that struck me the first time when I went to Sarajevo was, in fact, I have never seen so many minarets during all my trips, but what struck me was that the damage that was done was, fortunately, less than in other towns. There were other different intentions. There were different targets, and there was not any particular reason to attack the synagogues if you had the churches or the mosques. In Mostar, there is a synagogue that goes back many years, that was slightly damaged, but it has not acted as a synagogue for many, many years, since 1945.
