The Jewish component, which is a very important part for Bosnia, particularly as regards their memories because the Jewish population is very, very small, they suffered a lot during the Second World War and there is not a large percentage of Jews, therefore, they were not a particular target.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The court, Dr. Kaiser, thank you for your presentation. I see that the Prosecutor is making a sign to me. Would you like to add something, another question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, if I might, if I could just respond to Judge Riad's question regarding a possibility of legitimate military damage? At trial, the Prosecutor would be prepared to expand on the calendar that Dr. Kaiser mentioned as well as the geographical locations because when you put the time lines together with the geographical locations, what we would be prepared to show is that much of the damage occurred behind the frontlines so there could be no military purpose. Also many of the sacral sites were damaged in areas where there was little or no resistance whatsoever, so again there would be no military purpose. Finally, even in areas where there was resistance, such as in the town of Brcko, the mosques were fired upon when the fighting was actually in a different part of the city. So again there could be no military purpose. So we would be prepared to present this more detailed and extensive testimony when we go to trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, I would like to thank you for your presentation. Thank you on behalf of the International Tribunal. We are very grateful to you. This is the end of your presentation. We will adjourn until 4.30. (4.10 p.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time) (4.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, the court accepts the exhibits that you submitted in connection with the previous witness. So, if the Registrar would please take note of that for the case file? You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. As its next witness, the Prosecution would call Captain Patrick Rechner, please. CAPTAIN PATRICK ANTHONY RECHNER, called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please remain standing, and put on the head sets, if you would? Let us see, first, can you hear me, Captain? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Now you are going to remain standing to read the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Captain Rechner, you have been called by the Prosecution in connection with -- you do not need -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also speak French.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So let me repeat that. You have been called by the Prosecution as part of the public hearing in connection with the charges against Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic. You are before the International Criminal Tribunal. The Tribunal would ask you to speak without any fears and you will please proceed, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Captain, would you please statement your full name and spell it for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is captain Patrick Anthony Rechner. The first name Patrick is spelt P-A-T-R-I-C-K, my middle name is Anthony spelt A-N-T-H-O-N-Y, and my last name Rechner is spelt R-E-C-H-N-E-R.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Captain, you are currently serving in the Canadian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What is your rank and branch of service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Captain in the Infantry

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What languages do you speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I speak, I can say eight in different levels of fluency; English, French, Czech, Polish, Slovak, German, Russian and Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you serve in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you please take the court through your various assignments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served -- is that strictly in Bosnia-Herzegovina or throughout the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Throughout the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first served there as a member of the Canadian Battalion from February until May 1993 and western Slovenia, or UN protected area sector west. Then I returned for 12 months tour of duty as a UN military observer from July 1994 until July 1995. My first assignments as a UN military observer were in Zadar, in sector south, and I stayed there until December 1994 also working in Knin and Benkovac. Then at the end of December 1994, exactly 31st December 1994, I was posted to Pale where I had remained until 18th June 1994 -- correction, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You have served as a United Nations military observer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you just briefly explain to the court what are the responsibilities of a UN military observer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UN military observers have different responsibilities, depending on which mission they are employed in throughout the world. In the former Yugoslavia, our main task was to effect liaison between the different warring parties and also between the warring parties and the UN military command, that is, UNPROFOR. Also, we were unofficially dealing with the humanitarian organisations, trying to provide them with some assistance and developing local communities to aid their work. Our last job was to report directly to the Security Council on any conflict activity and on the full scope and type of conflict that was occurring wherever we could get access to in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How were you personally selected as a United Nations military observer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Canadian military officers, the requirement is to serve, to be minimum in the rank of captain and complete a minimum of six years of commissioned active service as an officer. In our case, we just applied to be selected as a UN military observer. Our military, regimental system or then branch of service then looks at the candidates and makes the choice and gives the names directly to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: After being selected as a military observer, where was it that you were first stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, I was for about two weeks in Zadar in Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Then where did you move?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then to Knin in sector south.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Then would you take us through that chronology again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. Zadar, those two weeks, it was just as a normal UN military observer doing patrolling duty. In Knin, I was there from the end of July 1994 until the beginning of November 1994. I was employed as the Chief Operations Officer for the UN military observer headquarters in Knin. Then from the beginning of November 1994 until the end of December 1994, I was a team leader stationed in Benkovac, that is in sector south as well, and my responsibility was for the southern half of the UN protected area of sector south.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At some point you were assigned to Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was on 31st December 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What was the period of your service in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Pale, I was there from that date until when I was released after the hostage taking on 18th June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What responsibilities did you have in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Pale, there were four military observers stationed there as part of the liaison team. Our duties involved passing letters between the UN and the Bosnian Serb government, and also between the UN and the Bosnian Serb military headquarters which was actually located in Han Pjesak, about 60 kilometres from Pale. Occasionally, we would also have some meetings with the local political leaders, but mostly it involved telephone calls and sending messages by fax. Then towards the second half of April, I took over as the team leader and Chief Liaison Officer to the Bosnian Serb government and the Military High Command, that is, the Bosnian Serb Military High Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Who were some of the leaders or individuals from the Pale administration that you would have contact with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The major figure was Professor Koljevic, the Vice President, because his other task or position that he filled was the Chairman of their government committee for co-operation with the UN and UNPROFOR. We also dealt directly with Dr. Karadzic's office, specifically with his secretary, Mira, and Mr. Jovan Zametica who was Mr. Karadzic's spokesman and political adviser. We also had some dealings with Mr. Kalinic, the Minister of Health.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How often did you communicate with these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Directly with Professor Koljevic, it was quite rare, but with his secretary, Zeca(?), it was almost on a daily basis and with Dr. Karadzic's office, that is, with his secretary, Mira, or Mr. Jovan Zametica, it was also on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Some time in May 1995 did you have a meeting with Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was either right at the end of April or beginning of May 1995, I went to see him in my capacity as the Chief UNMO Liaison Officer with Colonel Ermolajev, who was the Deputy Senior Regional Military Observer, that is, the Deputy of all of the observers working in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had a whole bunch of military observers that were blocked in the safe areas and were not allowed any access out either to rotate them or for leave. So we tried to gain the intervention of Professor Koljevic to assist us in working with the Bosnian Serb military to make an exception for some of these UNMOs to let them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened as a result of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a result of the meeting, Professor Koljevic did intervene and about one week or 10 days later we were able to get the UN military observers from the safe area of Zepa out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: That meeting occurred in late April or early May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened on 25th May 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 25th May 1995 was the day of the first NATO bombing of the bunkers on the outskirts of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you determine approximately how many bombs fell on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not able to determine exactly, but we heard two loud explosions and saw two large billows of smoke from locations, what we estimated about 10 kilometres south of our house in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What was in that general area where you saw the smoke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time we had no idea whether it was a military facility or something else. In fact we were not sure it was bombing because the size of the explosion and the cloud of dust and smoke that arose was much larger than we would normally expect from a single bomb dropped by an aircraft, that is a bomb of 1,000 or 2,000 pounds, but as we found out later the large size of the explosion and the large amount of smoke and dust was a result of the bunkers being hit in the secondary explosions inside the bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you see any damage to civilian structures on 25th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no damage. But if I can explain, on 25th May we were also confined to our accommodations. We did not have any freedom. We were told not to leave our accommodations, so we could not go out to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Where were your accommodations located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in the centre of Pale more or less, about 300 metres from the Bosnian Serb presidency, that is Dr. Karadzic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You did not see any damage in the immediate vicinity of your accommodations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: All right. What happened on the next day, 26th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day at about 10 o'clock the bombing was resumed. It looked to us it was the same targets as the previous days or the same general area, that is south, and we estimated about 10 kilometres. The only difference from the previous day was that it was much more intensive. We had counted throughout that morning from about 10 o'clock until about 11 o'clock about 12 explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Shortly after the bombing began on 26th did something occur outside your accommodations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, within about five or 10 minutes of the first bomb being dropped there were two shots that were fired just outside of our accommodations and some loud voices. Would you like me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What did do when you heard these shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I was not in our office. I was upstairs, so I just waited a few minutes to see what would happen. I did not here anything further and then I went downstairs to investigate what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When you went downstairs were you able to go into a section that was isolated from the office itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: . Yes, I think it may help if I describe our office and accommodations in Pale. We were living with a local family in their house. It was a three-storey house, that is three storeys including the ground floor. The family lived on the middle floor and we lived on the top floor. On the bottom floor there was on one side the living room and the kitchen and on the other side was our office which was a converted garage. So, I had gone down the stairs from the top floor which is the third level down to the main floor. There was a small door in the back of our office which was slightly ajar, so I looked in there and saw three armed individuals. Then I went into the kitchen to make some telephone calls trying to find out if these people had been sent there officially to protect us or whether they were just some local out for revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When you decided to make some calls who did you contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first person I called was Dr. Karadzic's office and I spoke with his secretary Mira and I explained to her that there were three people in our office armed, who had entered about 10 o'clock and asked her if she could send someone by to investigate what was going on. She asked me if -- first of all, she asked me what time they came, so I said about 10 minutes or so after 10 o'clock, which was about five minutes earlier of the time of my telephone call. She asked me if there were soldiers. So I said, well, it was difficult to tell because only one of them was dressed in a proper uniform, but she said, no, if they came shortly after 10 that they were sent officially. That was the first telephone call I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Why was your first reaction to call Karadzic's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all because we had been dealing directly with him and because we were worried that some people may be out to take revenge on us because of the bombing. We thought it was best to deal with the highest level. But we had also through Mr. Jovan Zametica, that is Mr. Karadzic's spokesman and senior political officer. We had the intervention of Mr. Karadzic in a previous incident to help us resolve hijacking that had occurred in trying to get our vehicle back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Now what happened after Karadzic's secretary confirmed to you that the men were there on official business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also wanted to confirm with Mr. Zametica himself, if I could get a hold of him, if he knew what was going on and also to inform him that we had some armed people in our office. So I called him in his hotel room at the Hotel Bistrica in the Jahorina area which is about 15 minutes drive from Pale. Mr. Zametica confirmed, saying that he had heard that something was being prepared to send some people into our office, that is sending some soldiers into our office. I asked him what he meant by that, and he said that he could only suggest that we be as co-operative as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: So you received confirmation from the accused Karadzic's secretary and also Karadzic's spokesman that the armed men were there on official business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Are UNMOs United Nations military observers armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, UN military observers are not armed. In fact that is what distinguishes us principally from the other UN forces in the former Yugoslavia. So we are not armed. We live and work in the local communities and we work in small international teams typically of six officers from all around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened after you confirmed with your two sources that the men were there on official business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was almost immediately as I put the phone down after speaking with Mr. Zametica that one of our interpreters who was in the office came out and called for me in a loud voice. So I came out of the kitchen. I asked her what she had wanted and she said I was needed in the office. So I followed her in the officer and there confronted three or at that time it was to armed men because the third one had gone outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How were the two men dressed and how were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was dressed in a typical camouflage uniform that the Bosnian Serb soldiers wear with a helmet as well. The other one had a red t-shirt and camouflage pants. Both of them had automatic weapons that are AK 47s and the one with the t-shirt had some hand grenades as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When the interpreter brought you to these two men what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told to sit down and then after a few seconds they told me to get in touch with my headquarters by radio and to put them through to my headquarters which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What took place once you got in touch with your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just explained to my headquarters that we had some armed people in our office and they wished to speak with them, so I passed the handset from the radio to the Bosnian Serb soldier who actually spoke perfect English. He explained to our headquarters that he wanted the bombings stopped immediately and if it was not going to be stopped that they would start executing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did this Serbian soldier have you make an additional call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because our office explained to them that the UN military observers had nothing to do with the bombing, that they were not able to do anything immediately. So then the soldier asked me to put him in touch with General Smith's office. That is General Rupert Smith who was the Commander of UNPROFOR at the time in Sarajevo. So I called his office with which we dealt quite regularly as well on our telephone and put the soldier in touch with General Smith's aide-de-camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you overhear the conversation that took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Bosnian Serb soldier also explained very angrily that he wanted the bombing stopped immediately, and he explained that from that moment on every bomb that would be dropped, for every bomb that would be dropped one of the UNMOs would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened after this call was concluded to General Smith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assumed that the aide-de-camp explained to him that it would take some time to get the bombing stopped, so we just waited and the Bosnian Serb soldier explained that his military commander would come in a few minutes and that we would just wait and that is what we did. About 10 minutes later, which would be about 11 o'clock that morning, a group of soldiers came led by a person whose name was something like Srdjan who was the Commander of this particular unit of which these two soldiers came in to our office initially, and the ones who initially made the telephone calls and the radio calls to our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was this unit part of the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume so, whether it was a regular or paramilitary unit I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken in our own vehicle to a location called Jahorinski Potok to be which is the location where the bunkers were, that is the bunkers that were hit the previous day and also that morning by the NATO air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When you arrived at Jahorinski Potok what was the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were held up at the main gate to the complex because it was locked and the soldiers present there did not have the key. So it took about 10 minutes or so before they could find someone to open it. In the meantime a group of civilians had gathered who had lived right on the outskirts of the bunkers. The situation was very tense. They were very angry seeing UN people because in their minds we were responsible for the bombing. One of the individuals broke away from the group and came to our vehicle, opened the door and assaulted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened when this individual assaulted you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fortunately our guards reacted quickly, so just after a couple of small punches and kicks he was pulled off. As he seemed to relax he quickly pulled out us his pistol, cocked it, that is chambered around, and tried to get a round or get a shot off at us. Again our guards reacted in time and prevented him from shooting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Now you mentioned there were bunkers at Jahorinski Potok. What did these bunkers contain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the bunkers were located I would say about 2 kilometres or so inside the complex and from what we could tell they contained mines, mortar and artillery ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were the soldiers able eventually to get access to the complex?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not by key though. As I mentioned, after about 10 minutes someone came and they managed to open the lock by smashing it with a hammer. We were taken into the complex but not immediately to the bunkers. We were first taken to some warehouses a few hundred metres inside the complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were you handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were handcuffed once we arrived at the warehouses and I assume we stopped there just to await final confirmation that the air strikes had been called off. Then I would say about 10 minutes or so after arriving at the warehouses we got the message by our radio in the vehicle that the air strikes had now been called off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Now while waiting at the warehouse did you have any contact with a Lieutenant Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was one Lieutenant Colonel from the Bosnian Serb army who was with us from the moment the group of soldiers, that is the second group of soldiers, arrived at our accommodations and he was filming the whole proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did he make any reference to a pistol he was carrying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, not only him but all of the soldiers were very angry, very hostile. This Lieutenant Colonel mentioned that even if the NATO air strikes -- well, I should mention first that he had explained we would be kept at the warehouses to prevent any NATO air strikes, but he added that even if we were not to be killed by any resumption of air strikes he would come by later in the day and shoot us personally. So he pulled out his revolver and showed us the handle on which he had two notches cut, explaining those two notches represented two people that he had killed and he would be very happy to have three more notches for the three officers and my team on his pistol as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: While you were in the area of the warehouse were you also forced to re-contact your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the first time was just to confirm after we got the message that the air strikes would be called off, to confirm that they were actually called off, and then we were loaded back in the vehicles and driven to the bunkers themselves. On our way there I was told to contact my headquarters and explain that we would die for the sake of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Who instructed you to make this statement to your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the Lieutenant Colonel who was filming the proceedings, and the one I mentioned had threatened to shoot us at the end of the day if the NATO air strikes did not kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did anyone mention or comment on why there was someone there filming the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one commented on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Now you were eventually moved to another area within the complex, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were moved from the warehouse to the actual bunkers where we were handcuffed. That was the only place we were moved around inside that complex on 26th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened when you were taken to the area near the bunkers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to -- there were four bunkers, two of which had been hit by the aerial bombs. Myself and the Russian military observer, Captain Pavel Teterevsky, I was handcuffed, he was tied to a lightning rod in front of the bunkers and the third UNMO Captain, Oli Zidlik, was handcuffed to the door of the bunker itself about 10 metres in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: So there were three of you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were three. I mentioned at the beginning that there were four military observers in my team. The fourth one was away on leave at the time. So there were only three of us in Pale on 25th and 26th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Now once the Serb soldiers handcuffed you to the lightning rod, how close were you to the ammunition bunkers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in front of one that had not been destroyed, about 10 metres in front of it, and that was 10 metres in front of Captain Zidlik who was handcuffed to the front door of that bunker, that is of that same bunker that had not been hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: About what time of the day was this when you were handcuffed to the lightning rod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say this would be close to about 11.30 that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you tell if any of the bunkers in the immediate vicinity had been hit by the bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had seen shell or bomb craters as well as the back half of one bunker which was to my right as I was facing it blown out, and the other one to my left had been hit from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were additional hostages eventually brought to the area where were you handcuffed to the lightning rod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at about 1 o'clock, 1300 hours that day, we saw team members from the other UN military observer team in Pale taken to the same complex driven by Bosnian Serb soldiers in their own, that is in the UN vehicles. This other team of military observers was a normal group of observers that fulfilled the functions of patrolling and monitoring conflict activity. They were stationed in Pale as well. So they had been rounded up at about 1300 hours and brought to the same complex where we were being used as human shields.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How many additional observers were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were altogether five.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What did the Serb soldiers do with these additional five observers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They put them in different locations throughout the complex. All four of them or four of the five I understand were kept in other areas close to the warehouses where we had been initially held up. The fifth was a Polish UNMO, Major Kalbarczyk, and he was taken further up the road past us to a bunker that we could not see about 300 metres away around a bend, but that had been hit that morning and where the ammunition was still exploding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: So, in your opinion, the Polish observer was placed in the most dangerous location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among us certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How long were you handcuffed to the lightning rod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my case it was about five and a half or six hours, that is from about 11.30 that morning until 5 o'clock that afternoon or shortly after 5 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At some point after being handcuffed to the lightning rod did some soldiers return to check on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They actually came first about one hour after we were handcuffed there just to give us some water, and then also when they brought the other military observers at 1300 hours they came by just to check on us to make sure we were still firmly handcuffed. Then at about 1430 or just before 1430 two soldiers came up to check on us. They were discussing amongst themselves whether they had enough time to go up further to check on the Polish UNMO who I had explained was about 300 metres away at the other ammunition bunker. These two soldiers had mentioned or one of the two soldiers was telling the other one that if they went up to check on the Polish observer they would not have enough time to get out of the area before 1430 hours which they explained was the time that the UN had announced that the air strikes would resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What language were these two soldiers speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These two soldiers were speaking Serbo-Croatian. I understood that and also Captain Oli Zidlik, the Czech observer from my team, he speaks fluent Serbo-Croat and he understood that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: While you were chained or handcuffed to the lightning rod, did any officials visit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were first I think it was about 1530 hours that afternoon, two groups of military officers, fairly senior, the top ones being of full Colonel rank, came by just to see us but they seemed more interested in the damage that had been caused by the air strikes. Then there was a group of civilians which I had assumed was a political delegation, and among them, that is among the civilian group, was also Jovan Zametica who I mentioned was Karadzic's spokesman and political adviser.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with Zametica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Zametica had stopped to chat with me. I had explained to him my surprise at the way we were treated roughly, that is in our capacity as their liaison team. I mentioned to him an incident earlier where the Bosnian Serb government and military had protested very vehemently against the forceful extradition of two liaison officers from the Bosnian Serb army in Goran Vakuf by the British UN forces. I explained to him, "In the light of your complaints about that, how do you explain the way that we are being treated?" He answered that obviously times had changed and he seemed content with what was happening or the way we were being treated, that is used as human shields, and he remarked: "I wonder what General Smith will do now?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At some point you were released from the lightning rod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was at about 5 o'clock in the afternoon. A group of two soldiers came by in one of our UN vehicles and took me and the Polish UNMO who was further up the road, 300 metres away, and we were transported to the radar site at Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: On the way did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not much. Once we pulled off the main road that goes to the hotels at Jahorina and pulled off that road on to a dirt track, we stopped and they blindfolded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What were your thoughts when they blindfolded you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to say. We were not sure what was happening, if we were being taken away to the executed as a reprisal for any air strikes or whether we were being taken to be detained somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: While riding in the vehicle on your way to the Jahorina radar site, Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.Pages 487 to 493. did you hear one of the Serbian soldiers in the car say anything about Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had four or five soldiers in the vehicle and they were talking amongst themselves, and one of them asked a question why we were going up to Jahorina and the other one answered that Mladic had told them that he wanted some UN people filmed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was this conversation in Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You understood that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Now eventually you arrived at Jahorina radar site, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I say Jahorina radar site because it was on Mount Jahorina later one of the other soldiers mentioned that they had a large radar complex on Mount Jahorina. I am not sure if the one I call Jahorina radar site is the main one or if it is just another site, but it was certainly in the area of Mount Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was that general area with the locations of the radars of any strategic importance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not an Air Force officer, so it is difficult for me to comment exactly, but certainly any operating radar site is of great strategic importance. Also later in our detention one of the guards mentioned that from the radar site on Jahorina the Bosnian Serb forces were able to monitor NATO aircraft taking off from bases in Italy and flying over the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened when you finally arrived at Jahorina radar site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The vehicle stopped. We were taken out of the vehicles. We were also handcuffed on the way up. The handcuffs were taken off and the blindfolds were taken off. The Lieutenant Colonel who had been filming us earlier in the day, that is the Lieutenant Colonel from the Bosnian-Serb army, he was present with his video camera plus two civilians, one a reporter whose name we later found out was Snezan Lalovic and whom we had met a couple of times later on during our hostage ordeal, and there was also a civilian camera man present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we got out of the vehicles. The blindfolds had been removed. Two of the soldiers took out their weapons and put on black masks. Then they took Major Kalbarczyk who was the Polish observer, to the actual radar dome and sat him down there, handcuffed him to the radar dome and conducted some sort of an interview. It was too far for me to be able hear what they were asking. That lasted about 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: After the completion of what appeared to be an interview, were you taken away from the radar site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They did not film me at the time up there, so we were loaded back in the vehicles, handcuffed and blindfolded and we were driven to the Hotel Bistrica. It was a funny situation, because it was completely relaxed. They took us to the main lounge of the hotel. They asked us if we would like anything, coffee or beer, so I had a coffee and I think Major Kalbarczyk also had a coffee. It was also with the soldiers who had taken us, so there were the two of us, the observers, the reporters, Snezan Lalovic, and about five or six soldiers. We had waited there. I assumed the soldiers were waiting for instructions on what to do next with us. After about 15 or 20 minutes Major Kalbarczyk and I were taken with about three other soldiers to have supper in the hotel which was actually quite a nice meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: After your meal, were you taken to another location to spend the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were taken to a military barracks which is the military barracks where we were held from then on throughout the 24 days of our hostage ordeal. It was called Koran barracks according to the local soldiers. It was right on the outskirts of Pale. It was there that we met the other military observers from the Pale area with whom we had had no contact at all during that day. For us it was also a sense of relief to be there, because the soldiers had explained to us earlier we would be spending the night handcuffed in the different locations within the bunker complex, and that they would make some arrangements later on just to give us some blankets so that we would not freeze overnight. It was, as I mentioned, quite a relief when we found we would actually be able to spend the night in a real building and not out in front of the bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How many hostages were there in this barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time there were 10 of us. There were the three officers from my team, five officers from the other UN military observer team from Pale and two officers from the team in Gorbavica which is a suburb of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were you moved to different location the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the next day. It was on the third day, 28th May. Later in the afternoon we were moved from the building where we had been had been for the first three days which was a room in a large dormitory building to a small guard house within the same complex near the main gate. It was in the small guard house where we remained from 28th May until 18th June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: On May 28th were you allowed to go back to the liaison office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: And what did you try to do when you arrived at the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had gone back there. They allowed two of us to go back to our accommodations and also the accommodations for the other observer team in Pale to pick up some change of clothes and things to wash with, toiletries and so on that we would need whilst staying at this military barracks. When I entered our office one of our interpreters was there because I had instructed our interpreters to continue working as we were being led away the first stage of the hostage ordeal. So this interpreter was there. I had instructed her to fax a message to our headquarters in Sarajevo telling them that we were fine. It was at that point that our landlord, Mr. Danjlo Savac who also happened to be in the office, was able to understand that I was instructing my interpreter to fax something. He immediately interrupted the proceedings stating that Mr. Krajicnik, that is the speaker of the Bosnian-Serb Assembly, had called him and explained that we were not under any circumstances to be allowed to make any telephone calls or fax any messages. The landlord, Mr. Danjlo Savic, mentioned to me that I was to do as I was told and if everything would work out in three or four days we would all be set free.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How is it that Krajicnik would have this type of contact with your landlord?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our landlord was an old friend of Mr. Krajicnik from before the war. We had actually been able to use Mr. Krajisnik's influence earlier when our vehicle had been stolen, we suspect by the local police, to get the this vehicle returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Now at some point after you had been taken hostage, did you learn of some allegations that the Serbs had been making against you and the military observers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard from some of the other observers, I think it was either the end of the first day or the beginning of the second day, sorry, toward the end of the second day when they had been in their accommodations, that their interpreters told them that they had seen on local television screens our images and the local television explained to the public that we, that is myself, Captain Zidlik and Captain Teterevsky, that is our observer team, we had been the UN people who were actually involved in guiding in the air strikes, that is acting as forward air controllers, which is an absolute lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were even capable of doing that type of observation if you ever wanted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. First of all, none of us was trained for that sort of activity. We had none of the technical equipment such as radios or the observation equipment required to guide in the air strikes, and we were not even able to see the target from our accommodations. As I mentioned earlier, those bunkers were about 10 kilometres away. When I had said we observed the explosions, all we had seen was we had heard the noise and then seen the clouds of smoke and dust 10 kilometres away rise up from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you ever confront anyone about these false allegations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we confronted the reporter Snezan Lalovic whom we had seen on second day about it, and also later on when he came to see us on 31st May. Mr. Lalovic explained that because the other sides in the war were lying in their propaganda, the Serbs also had to lie and that it was perfectly justified for them to be lying and accusing us of such activity in order to support their propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: On or around May 29th did you attempt to get in touch with Kolevic's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 29th May I and another military observer, we were sent to our accommodations again to pick up some things that we had forgotten from the first couple times, and also I believe to do some laundry. We had made an arrangement with the guards that every few days one or two of us accompanied by two of the guards would go to our accommodations to drop off our dirty laundry to get cleaned by our landlord's family because we had already paid for that month's rent. So, we first went to the accommodations for the other observer team in Pale, and in their accommodations one of my interpreters who was off duty, she was present, and as I knew that we would be going in a few minutes from that accommodations to my own accommodations, I had asked my interpreter to call my office and instruct the interpreter who was on duty from my office to call Professor Koljevic's office and ask Professor Koljevic's secretary, whose name is Zeca to call our accommodations about five minutes later. I mentioned "five minutes later" because five minutes should have coincided with my arrival at my accommodations. So when we left the accommodations of the -- to make it easier I will call the other UNMO team in Pale Sierra Echo 1, that was their radio call sign. So when we left Sierra Echo 1's accommodations and arrived at my own accommodations, as I walked in the door the telephone rang. On the other line was Professor Koljevic's secretary. My interpreter who had picked up the phone turned to the guard and said that Professor Koljevic's secretary would like to speak to me. The guard said, fine, and the receiver from the telephone was passed to me and I spoke with Professor Koljevic's secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were you able to set up any sort of meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Up till that point I had thought that perhaps the whole hostage taking or at least the way we were treated may have been a big mistake because of our good working relationship before with the Bosnian Serb government and the military. So I had asked if Zeca could arrange for me to see Professor Koljevic very soon, that it was have very urgent for me to speak with him. She said she would organise it for the next day. Then she asked me to put the guard who was with me, and his name was Captain Radovan Vojvodic. So she, that is Zeca, Professor Koljevic's secretary, instructed Captain Vojvodic that there would be a meeting organised the following day for me to attend with to see Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were you able to eventually have a meeting with Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Much, much eventually. The next day nothing happened. Captain Vojvodic, the guard, mentioned that he was unable to get in touch with Professor Koljevic's office and similar stories or explanations were offered over the following days. It was not until three days before being released, that is on 15th June, that Professor Koljevic had finally arranged for me to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When you finally had the opportunity to see Koljevic, how did the meeting go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My main concern was for us to be able to make contact with our next of kin, and then also discuss with him some of the rougher or more difficult aspects of our treatments, and also to discuss with him what sort of future working relationship could be established between the UN military observers and the Bosnian Serb government in the light of our very poor treatment as hostages. In that meeting we discussed that. Professor Koljevic mentioned that as a result of the crisis which was the result of the bombing itself, that the relations between the Bosnian Serb government and the UN were at an all time low, and that a completely new working relationship would have to be established. He also justified the hostage taking, saying that although he understood that it was very difficult for us, he added that the Bosnian Serb government needed to send a very strong message to the UN and used the analogy of an electric shock, explaining that in case of certain medical conditions an electric shock may, although kill a person in some cases, may cure him. So they said they needed to send an electric shock to the UN to try to cure the relations between them and the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that may be an appropriate place to end for the day.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, it is 5.30. The hearing is adjourned. We shall go on tomorrow morning, Captain, at 10 o'clock. (5.30 p.m.) (The court adjourned until the following day) 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
